speechtext: The House resumed from Tuesday, September 26, consideration of the motion of Mr. Mulroney that Bill C-29, an Act to establish the Department of Forestry, to amend the Forestry Development and Research Act and amend the Forestry Development and Research Act and to make related amendments to other Acts, be read the second time and referred to a ligislative committee.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: Debate. The Hon. Member for Glengarry-Prescott-Russell (Mr. Boudria).

speakerposition: Deputy Whip of the Liberal Party
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I welcome this opportunity today to take part in the debate on Bill C-29, an Act to establish the Department of Forestry. You may rest assured that I have no intention of voting against this Bill. It would be tantamount to voting against trees, or against nature, and I am not against nature any more than I am against motherhood or apple pie. I don't think you have any reason to worry about that. And I am sure my colleague opposite is delighted to see that I intend to support this Bill.

Canada needs Bill C-29 but, of course, it needs more than that bill. When I say that it needs Bill C-29, it needs it because the legislation will consolidate many government activities pertaining to forestry which are right now spread among a variety of different ministries. When I
say that it needs more than Bill C-29, or it needs Bill C-29 and much more, I mean that the forestry minister will not have much power under this legislation, simply because he or she will have to obtain funding from other departments in order to embark on federal-provincial reforestation programs, in order to arrive at agreements between the federal government and the provinces, and also in order to actually get the funding to do his job as a minister.
I am going to touch on the federal-provincial agreements in a moment, but first I would like to talk about an experience in my own constituency.

Mr. Speaker, about 50 kilometres from Ottawa, in the beautiful riding of Glengarry-Prescott-Russell, there is a forest, the Larose Forest, which covers a hundred square kilometres and where 18 million trees have been planted, most of them by hand. All this was the work of a genius by the name Ferdinand Larose. In 1900, Mr. Larose, a resident of the area and agronomist for the counties of Prescott and Russell, had the brillant idea, Mr. Speaker, to start a reforestation project in what could be called the desert area of Bourget. This area southeast of Ottawa had become practically barren as a result of erosion and other factors.
Mr. Speaker, a tree planting program started in 1928. The program continues today, and Larose Forest is now the largest reforestation project in Ontario.

It bears repeating that near this city we have the largest man-made forest in Ontario, only some 50 kilometres from Parliament Hill. If you can imagine that visionary agronomer, Mr. Larose, who in 1928, particularly given his profession, was telling farmers to get off the land, to sell it to the government so it could be replanted with trees. Needless to say, there were probably some people in the community who wanted to chase that gentleman right out of town for coming up with a scheme like that.

Government Orders
Imagine what the people in the village, the merchants, and so on, were thinking, when farms that were previously occupied became vacant at the encouragement of this man Ferdinand Larose. It seems, in retrospect of course, that he was right. He had the bright idea of creating this forest in an area which was practically a desert.
I said moments ago that I would come back to this issue of reforestation and federal-provincial agreements. The reason I want to bring this to your attention is as follows: The Canada-Ontario Forest Resource Development Agreement, or COFRDA for short, has now expired. That agreement which was in place contributed to the tune of $150 million to reforestation programs in the province of Ontario. It was because of programs such as COFRDA and others in the past that the replanting of the Larose forest and probably many other similar projects were made possible.
As we are here discussing the creation of a new department of forestry-which I favour of course-I cannot help but condemn the government for the fact that forestry has suffered an 11.9 per cent cutback in 1989-1990.1 am sure the Minister of Transport is terribly upset by this and that the cause of this, of course, is the budgetary cutbacks inflicted upon these departments by the Minister of Finance who is sitting almost immediately in front of me.

Mr. Speaker, forty-seven person-years were cut in this ministry, a reduction of 3.5 per cent. Today, we are talking about establishing a department of forestry but I think we should recall that, under the Tory Government, there has been no particular concern for our forests, and in fact there have been major cutbacks.

Mr. Speaker, I wanted to talk about COFRDA, the agreement which has expired and which I hope the Minister of Finance, who is listening attentively, will negotiate with his provincial counterpart and renew that federal-provincial agreement, COFRDA, with the province of Ontario.
Let me tell the Minister what this has created in our province. I invite him, by the way, to come and visit the Larose forest, 50 kilometers east of Ottawa. He can jump in his limousine and I will show him this forest. I
will gladly do it this afternoon as a matter of fact, Mr. Speaker. But let me tell you of some of the benefits of this agreement.
Over the last five years in the province of Ontario COFRDA has accomplished the regeneration of 110,000 hectares of land; the tending of 59,000 acres; the site preparation of 113,000 acres; and the purchase of 165 million tree seedlings. Indeed, COFRDA has contributed tremendously toward the reforstation of our province.
Unfortunately, the time allocated to MPs to speak today is shorter than usual and I will have to conclude my remarks very soon. I will not be able to further state to the minister how important it is for him to contribute to this federal-provincial agreement in Ontario. I hope that I have gone some distance in convincing him, and I know that my colleagues will continue to do so over the next few minutes.

Mr. Speaker, in concluding, I would like to say that today in Larose Forest, the trees are about 100 feet high. Those beautiful trees, the white pine we see in our area, were planted thanks to people with vision. People like Ferdinand Larose, people who wanted to make a contribution and who knew it was important to preserve this forest and to replant it.
My message to the House and especially to the Minister of Finance is that the Government should stop these cuts in the forestry department and enter into an agreement as soon as possible with the province of Ontario and other provinces who also need them, so that we can keep up the good work done by Ferdinand Larose and other Canadian pioneers.

Am I correct in believing that today, contrary to the other days this week, and we can take the example of the Liberal Party, they will use the 20 minutes as they see fit, and at the end of 20 minutes, a 10 minute question and comment period. There will not be ten-five, ten-five. It will be 20 among two or three speakers. Very well.
Government Orders
Agreed.

Mr. Speaker, I would like to return to the issue at hand. I am very pleased to speak on this legislation before us. I say that because it has been long overdue. The Prime Minister (Mr. Mulroney) promised the Department of Forestry in the 1984 general election. We thought, on this side of the house, that he had forgotten, but luckily his memory came back.
Bill C-29 will, in part, restore faith in the forest industry that it has not been overlooked. The industry will be assured of a voice at the cabinet table. While this legislation creates a new department of forestry, there remain a few questions which we need to have addressed.
One of the main concerns with this piece of legislation is the lack of an adequate budget. The department of forestry saw its 1989-90 budget cut by 11.9 per cent. This does not seem fair as other natural resource programs received increases in their budgets.
It seems to me that the government is not committed to providing leadership in the development of one of Canada's most precious resource. The government needs to inject more funds into this new department if Canada is to become a leading nation in the area of reforestation.
At a time when Canada lags behind in reforestation, what does the government do? It cuts the forestry budget and slashes 47 person-years along with it. The forestry department will need increased funds and staff resources in order to catch up with other leading nations. The creation of a new forestry department must go hand in hand with adequate financial resources. Furthermore, the Minister of Forestry must be given total control over the future of his department. It will not work if he has to go to other departments and agencies for funding.
Canada's forestry industry makes a significant contribution to the Canadian economy. Canada has the second largest stock of softwood lumber in the world after the U.S.S.R. It is the third largest producer of softwood lumber products after the United States and the U.S.S.R. It is the largest exporter of lumber products: one third of its pulp exports, 63 per cent of its newsprint and nearly half of its lumber. These are significant statistics and we must look at what the government has done to this vital sector of the Canadian economy.

Government Orders
In 1986, after mounting pressure from the United States, the government decided to impose a 15 per cent export tax on all softwood lumber products. This measure has been a sore spot for the forest industiy. In northern Ontario the 15 per cent export tax has had a devastating effect on the softwood lumber industiy. It has also caused some concern to the 30 single industiy towns that need this resource for employment.
In February of this year members of the northern Ontario Liberal caucus travelled extensively in order to hear firsthand from the lumber industry, labour, and municipal governments. The witnesses repeatedly told us that the 15 per cent export tax will continue to force closures and lay-offs. We were told that the expansion and modernization projects have had to be put on hold because of this situation.
There have been some major economic changes since the imposition of this export tax which warrant a review of the situation. The U.S. dollar has depreciated by more than 18 per cent. There has been an increase in Ontario stumpage and area charges. Canadian exports are lower than they were pre-1986 and the lumber industry is faced with depressed prices.
The task force was told by industry representatives that with the signing of the free trade agreement the softwood lumber export tax should not exist in the free trade environment. McKenzie Forest Products in Sioux Lookout, a very large industiy and a large company in my riding, kept four trucks busy hauling finished softwood lumber products to the Minneapolis-St. Paul market just to the south of my riding. When the 15 per cent export tax was imposed, this market was lost. Now McKenzie Forest Products ships its lumber to southern Ontario.
The additional transportation charges have eroded profits it would have otherwise received had it been able to keep the U.S. market. The imposition of a further 9 per cent on transportation services under the goods and services tax will further erode potential profits. I suspect that we will see further sawmill closures and many more lay-offs as a result.
The government must demonstrate leadership in the area of reforestation and management of this resource. The forest is capable of providing employment for many future generations if the will of the government is such. To quote a representative from Canadian Pacific Forest
Products in Dryden: "It was a political decision to initiate the 15 per cent countervailing duty, so it will take a political solution to remove it". For the small, rural and northern regional economies, it is imperative that this government support the softwood lumber industry by eliminating this export charge.
I read in the July 27 edition of The Ottawa Citizen that the Minister of Forestry stated that his department has prepared a proposal which would be sent to the Americans to end the export tax. The minister was quoted in the article as stating that he would present them with a proposition to test the ground before we send them a termination notice.
This was a welcome statement, but I find it kind of scary because we do not know what the Americans will say. We ask the Minister, will he succumb to U.S. pressure once again, or will he demonstrate leadership by telling the Americans that we cannot agree with this tax in the spirit of the free trade agreement? He, as Minister of Forestry, has a responsibility to Canada's forests and the industiy.
A year ago this month a green ribbon review was held at the Great Lakes Forestry Centre in Sault Ste. Marie to look at the achievements and impacts of the Canada- Ontario Forest Resource Development Agreement. The review concluded that the agreement has had significant impacts on Ontario forests. There has been more forest management activity and employment because of it. The agreements have also ensured the viability of the forest industry, especially in northern Ontario where the economic survival of some 30 communities is directly dependent on the forest industry.
When the Province of Ontario signed the Forest Resource Development Agreement in 1984, it made a long-term commitment to managing a sustainable forest resource. The federal government's inaction is jeopardizing forest renewal programs in six provinces. It is undoing everything that has been achieved in the last five years if it persists in delaying the renewal of these agreements.
In 1987, the National Forest Sector Strategy, endorsed by the Canadian Council of Forest Ministers and Canada's First Ministers, urged this government to continue its spending commitments to forest resource development agreements with the provinces.

Maybe the government needs to be reminded of the forestry agreement achievements in Ontario over the past five years. As well as providing nearly one quarter of the funds for Ontario's regeneration program, the agreement helped to improve management practices on private woodlots and it has promoted integrated resource management for multiple use.
The agreement helped build some 300 kilometres of access roads which are vital to forest renewal operations. More important, the agreement funded forest management projects with 40 Ontario Indian bands. This has led to jobs for the aboriginal people. Ontario has a proud record of achievements as a result of the forestry agreement. Approximately 80 per cent of its forest management program is delivered by the private sector. Nurseries, tree planting, and road building are examples. There is no question that the Canada-Ontario agreement has played a key role in stimulating private sector involvement.
In a speech to the Ontario Forestry Association's annual meeting in February 1989, the then Natural Resources Minister for Ontario said, and I quote: "We cannot sustain this momentum without a new development agreement. Without it and without the continuity that a new agreement would provide, we jeopardize our future achievements and future gains. Without the federal contribution the amount of forest we regenerate each year simply will not be as high." By continuing to refuse to negotiate a new agreement the federal government will further damage its already tarnished reputation internationally.
The signing of a new Canada-Ontario Forest Resource Development agreement is vital to the economy of many small communities in my riding, many of which depend solely on the forest industry. In the Auditor General's report to Parliament, he urged that Canada's forest renewal efforts be strengthened with more funds and better management. He warned that Canada is not getting ahead in renewing its forests, despite sharp increases in provincial funding and co-operative cost sharing agreements. The provinces and the forestry industry need a long-term commitment from this government in the areas of forest regeneration and sustainable development. Canada's forests can continue to provide economic benefits and employment for genera-

tions to come, if they are properly managed. The Minister of Forestry must move quickly before Canadian forests suffer irreparable damage.
In order for the new Department of Forestry to achieve its goals in managing Canada's most precious natural resource, it must be provided with adequate funding and staff resources.
I urge the Minister of Forestry to talk to his colleagues and allow them to act responsibly on behalf of the people of Canada so that future generations of this country will have the kind of forests and forest regeneration that it needs.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of State (Forestry)
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I would like to thank the Hon. Member for Glengarry-Prescott-Russell (Mr. Boudria) for his unconditional support for the Forestry Bill. I also urge him to ask his colleagues, especially those who will sit on the legislative committee, to deal with this legislation very quickly so that it can be passed as soon as possible.
The Hon. Member for Glengarry-Prescott-Russell, Mr. Speaker, was concerned that the federal Government seemed to be forgetting about forests, at least according to him.
I would simply remind him that from 1984 until today, the federal Government-that is, the Progressive Conservative Government-has increased its budgets for silviculture by over 300 per cent. I think that is concrete action that should be pointed out, especially by our colleagues opposite.
I know that the Hon. Member for Glengarry-Prescott-Russell and his colleague boasted about the Cana-da-Ontario agreement. I must remind them, however, that this agreement was signed by the Progressive Conservative Government.
Also, the Hon. Member for Glengarry-Prescott- Russell is concerned about the effect the new Department will have. I would remind him that the new Department-that is, the one now represented by the Minister of State for Forestry (Mr. Oberle)-will no longer be a Department of State; therefore, it will report directly to the Prime Minister.

September 29, 1989
Government Orders
Moreover, the Forestry Bill is intended first and foremost to update the regulations on wood under which Forestry Canada manages forest areas together with other federal Departments.
The new Bill will also make it possible to extend the application of these regulations beyond experimental forest areas. It will enable the Minister and the Department-and I think it is important for my colleagues opposite to understand this-to conclude agreements with individuals, organizations and governments. I refer to the famous forestry development agreements with each province. The Minister will be authorized to do so, as provided in clause 9 of the Bill.
It also provides for the tabling in the House of an annual report on the status of forestry resources and their contribution to the Canadian economy.
Also, Mr. Speaker, what is new with the Department is that under its mandate, it will oversee the development and coordination of forestry policies and programs nationally. It will also carry out and encourage forestry research and development. We know how important research and development are for the future and survival of Canadian forestry, both for local and for export markets.
So in summarizing these facts, I think in all sincerity and honesty, beyond partisanship, Mr. Speaker, that our Liberal and New Democratic colleagues will make it their duty to act diligently, first, to complete second reading and, second, to move quickly and smoothly in the legislative committee to have this Bill passed as soon as possible. For as both Liberals and New Democrats have said so well, we need this legiation as soon as possible so that the Forestry Department can have a free hand in its negotiations with the federal Departments concerned with forestry and with the provinces and the whole industry, for the sake of the harmonious development of forestry in Canada.

speakerposition: Deputy Whip of the Liberal Party
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am not sure there was a question. Perhaps it was just a comment.

I should like to respond to some of the points raised by my colleague opposite.
First, concerning co-operation on the part of the Official Opposition to pass this measure at the earliest opportunity, the fact that we have readily agreed to reduce our speeches by half so as to speed up the process is, I would suggest, a sure sign of the good faith of the Official Opposition. What we want of course is to give Members who have significant observations to make to do just that without unduly delaying the Bill. This is why we too have shortened our speeches.

In terms of the federal government commitment to forestry, the member has stated that there were federal-provincial agreements and that the minister was empowered to continue working at them. But I want to repeat what I said before. Since last summer, there is no such thing as a federal-provincial agreement on forestry for the province of Ontario. The previous one was in the area of $150 million over five years, toward replanting forests, projects such as the one I described in my own riding. Right now there is no money. The Minister of Finance is sitting right across from us and I hope he is listening attentively to this. I hope he instructs his colleagues to get on with it and to provide the province of Ontario with the federal government participation so we can continue doing so.
In terms of the federal government's commitment toward forestry, it is contrary to what we have just heard. I will just give you one instance of lack of commitment. The newly created independent forestry budget was reduced from $235 million to $207 million. I believe this is for the province of British Columbia. That is a net cut here of some $28 million. That is not what I call commitment.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: Questions and comments. The Hon. Member for Manicouagan (Mr. Langlois).

Mr. Speaker, just a brief remark to remind my colleague from Glengarry-Prescott-Russell (Mr. Boudria) that, pursuant to clause 9, one of the responsibilities of the Minister will be to enter into agreements or arrangements with any person, body or government. He will have enough authority to discharge his duties. This means that the Minister may enter into agreements with the provinces, including agreements similar to ERDA subsidiary agreements. He can exercise that power with the approval of the Governor in Council.
September 29, 1989

Mr. Speaker, perhaps I might say in passing that the federal Government has just concluded agreements with New Brunswick under which the province will receive $91 million. It had received $77 million under the previous agreement, so this is a considerable increase in the federal Government's share in the development of forestry in New Brunswick. Similarly, Nova Scotia will get $45 million under a two-year agreement, again a significant increase over the funding made available under previous agreements.
In short, Mr. Speaker, the new Minister and his department will have full authority so sign agreements and support the growth of Canada's forest sector.

speakerposition: Deputy Whip of the Liberal Party
speechtext:
In response to that argument, which was also directed to me, Mr. Speaker, it is true that the Minister can sign agreements with the province, but he has to go to another department, and that is even worse, he has to go to a number of departments to get the money. Yes, but this works out to the same thing. The minister may sign any agreement he likes, but in the case of agreements where funds are not involved, he needs authority. That is not very good. The fact is that the entire exercise is directed by others, not by the department. Here is an example. In the case of an agreement with the Atlantic provinces, the Minister of Public Works will be authorized to release the funds. In the case of the western provinces it will be the Minister responsible for grains. In the case of Ontario the purse strings will be held by the Minister of Regional Industrial Expansion and Member for Calgary. That is the way things work under the new legislation, Mr. Speaker, so it is not perfect by any means.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: Resuming debate. The hon. member for Edmonton East.

Mr. Speaker, I would like to start with some general comments on the bill, by noting that it was in fact the New Democrats who proposed a separate ministry of forestry in 1983.1 note as well that in 1984 the leader of the Liberal Party at the time opposed that suggestion by the New Democrats. I am glad to see that in the intervening five years the Liberals have come around to see the wisdom of the New Democrat position. It happens from time to time. In fact the Canadian political historic record shows that it happens quite often.
I would note as well that the Conservative Party promised a forestry department in the 1984 election. Obviously certain contingencies intervened and they were, how shall I put this, prevented from making good on that promise in the entire period of their first term. So, they were in the happy position of being able to use the promise again in the 1988 election, which of course they did, and I must say to their credit this time they have acted upon it. This is sufficient to render it not quite but almost unique in that entire panoply of promises that the Conservatives advanced at the 1988 general election.
However, we went through that first term of Tory government from 1984 to 1988 and it was drag, drag, drag. There was no action on the creation of a department whatsoever. Now, in its second term, it seems incredibly hasty in pushing this bill through the Commons as quickly as it can. It is a remarkable turnabout, and one that the New Democrats at least are not terribly comfortable with. As my dear grandmother used instruct me as well-she was a very wise woman-anything worth doing is worth doing well.

September 29, 1989
Government Orders
So, instead of rushing this bill through the House, we New Democrats would suggest that at the very least thorough consideration ought to be accorded it in this House. As well, we would sincerely suggest along with many other interested Canadians that a range of public consultations on the bill be undertaken.
If I may, I would like to quote from the September 1989, No. 23 Newsletter of the Canadian Institute of Forestry where they note that the CIF recommends that there be public consultation in developing the new forestry act. Obviously that recommendation is no longer actionable. However, they recommend further:
-that the Standing Committee on Forestry and Fisheries be given legislative responsibility for review of the proposed legislation and that the committee hold public hearings in Ottawa and across the country. In this way interested groups and individuals will have an opportunity to make their views known concerning the federal role in the forestry sector.
A most admirably sensible suggestion, Mr. Speaker, and one which, if the government is serious about producing the best possible department of forestry, I am certain it will want to pursue.
Such consultations can be especially important given recent events and the growing importance of forestry in areas not previously known for it, like my home province of Alberta. There are huge new projects being proposed especially in the pulp and paper realm in the province of Alberta. In their wake, these new projects are creating growing environmental concerns.
Among those developments, in the light of which this bill and this new forestry department must be seen, are the unfortunate cut-backs in federal funding for forestry related matters that we have experienced. As was reported in that national newspaper The Globe and Mail on May 17 of this year the minister himself said that, excluding FRDAs his department will have $207 million to spend this year. This is nearly a $28 million drop from forestry expenditures last year.
I understand the members across the way have been arguing that this is not a cut-back, that in fact this is an enhancement. Such a cavalier approach to the English language do them no credit but we will, of course, leave it to their constituents this instance.
In the same story the hon. minister is reported as saying that funds for FDRAs would come from general regional development allocations, themselves slated for cuts. So even in this instance we have a bit of trouble with the usage across the way.
Finally, it is noted that the Western Diversification Agency will bear responsibility for funding the FRDAs with the provinces which fall within the jurisdiction of that agency. In total, the finance minister's budget papers showed a drop from $1.4 billion for regional development spending-and this with regard to the Western Diversification Office-during the current 1989-90 fiscal year to about $1 billion annually over the next four years. The government may argue if it wishes that this is not a cut, but I think it will have trouble convincing Canadians of that.
As well, even allowing that there is substantial but reduced funding for FRDAs out there, it must be borne in mind that that funding is to be delivered through the regional development vehicles and through the FRDAs. We have a situation in which as of March 31 this year, six Forestry Resource Development Agreements have expired. These are with my home province of Alberta, with Saskatchewan, Manitoba, Ontario, and New Brunswick-a new deal has been agreed to in principle with New Brunswick, it must be noted-and with Nova Scotia, for a total of $420 million.
The programs and jobs related to these programs are thereby threatened. It is greatly to be hoped, in fact it is reasonably to be expected, that the programs will be renewed. It is greatly to be hoped that they will be enhanced. But we have no guarantee of that. Such a guarantee must be forthcoming if we are to take the government's protestations about its desires for a new forestry department seriously. New Democrats have been vigorous in calling for the renewal of these programs. We will continue to be vigorous to that end.
There is another factor in light of which the growing importance of forestry and the proposal for the establishment of a forestry department must be viewed. That is the serious concern that establishing this new department will not be accompanied by the changes necessary to make it a sufficiently significant player within the ranks of the government.
September 29, 1989

The Conservative Government is using new agencies to act as the vehicle for federal-provincial economic development agreements, including the FDRAs. In my part of the country, that is, as I have noted, the Western Diversification Office. It controls funding for forestry programs in western Canada and the FDRAs are funded out of the WDO budget.
The forestry minister has to seek funds from western Diversification before he can negotiate with provinces to establish agreements. In other words, the decision-making power over who will get FDRAs and what those FDRAs will contain does not rest with the minister. In the first instance, that decision rests with the Western Diversification Office, which it must be noted has a great deal else on its plate. So what does this tell us about the importance that this government places on its new department and its minister? It tells us that it and he are second string. That is unfortunate because the economic ministries are sort of second-level treasury boards, and the minister has to deal with them for funding of his major programs.
The New Democrats are insistent that the department of forestry must have direct control over its own programs and its own initiatives. There is no substitute for this if we are to take the government's program at all seriously.
There are problems with the bill. There are problems with the department that the bill proposes to create. It is nothing that cannot be fixed. It is not an irreversible situation. But the government must listen, and not just to us on the opposition benches. The government must listen to the people of Canada, especially those with direct interest in forestry, if it is to improve this bill as it must be improved before it becomes law. But the government must listen, not just to us on the opposition benches, but to the people of Canada, especially those with a direct interest in forestry, if they are to improve this bill, as it must be improved, before it becomes law.
While we are on the topic of forestry, and given the importance of this issue in Alberta and the likelihood that there will not be many chances to address this issue in the House at this sitting, I would like to mention a few related matters that concern my constituents and the people of Alberta generally.
Government Orders
The forestry projects that are coming in Alberta, especially the major pulp and paper projects, have been the subject of considerable concern in that province. The Daishowa plant near Peace River is to be constructed with the help of a $9.5 million contribution from the Western Diversification Office. When this plant proposal was announced, many people were concerned that there had not been a proper environmental assessment review. They were right, there had not been. There were no public hearings.
The company prepared an environmental report, an impact statement, for the provincial environment department. The report did not even consider the cumulative effects on Alberta's environment of the contribution that the Daishowa plant would make to pollution in the province in light of that pollution which will be contributed by all the other proposed plants and those currently in place.
In fact, there are, as a consequence of that cumulative effect, which it is reasonable to anticipate, serious concerns about the biological oxygen demand levels in the rivers affected, principally the Athabasca river, but as well the Peace river, and about the dioxin and furan emissions from those plants. Since there was no proper environmental impact assessment, construction went ahead without these concerns being heard, much less addressed. In fact, Daishowa was granted a forestry management agreement for the mill on land claimed by the Lubicon people who are currently in the midst of a very serious, lengthy dispute with the federal government. The Daishowa plant was granted land out from underneath them; a most serious development and one that does neither of the governments involved any credit whatsoever.
I should note that one of the other major mills being proposed for Alberta is the Alberta-Pacific mill, which is to be located on the Athabasca river. The review by Alberta-Pacific was, it must be said, much better than the review undertaken by Daishowa. There is, for example, a joint federal-provincial co-operative approach to environmental assessment in this instance.
In fact, I will quote from the release of the Minister of Environment Canada, Release No. PR-HQ-089-34, dated July 19, in Ottawa.
He notes that he and Mr. Klein announced a federal-provincial environmental review of the proposed Alberta-Pacific kraft paper mill in northern Alberta. He said that the terms of reference of the review board will emphasize the need to assess cumulative impacts from the Alberta-Pacific and other mills on all downstream interests.

September 29, 1989
There we have it, a reasonable approach in this instance, assuming the review to be a thorough and effective one. What was lacking in Daishowa in this regard, at least, we find at Alberta-Pacific, and that is a good thing because there remain serious concerns.
I would note, as well that under this review for Alberta-Pacific, public hearings will be held. Their effect is yet to be judged, but the hearings themselves will be held. Intervener funding will be offered and, as I said, the cumulative effects of the mills on the river system is to be examined.
Why is that so important? It is because there are very, very serious concerns about the cumulative effect of biological oxygen demand occasioned by the operations of these pulp mills. In fact, just in the last week, the Alberta environment department released the results of an 18-month study on the Athabasca river that forecast that the river's oxygen level will stay above Alberta's set requirements for oxygen levels in that river only if stringent new standards are implemented and followed.
There are environmental groups in the province, including the Alberta Fish and Game Association, who are convinced that the measures proposed by Alberta environment are themselves inadequate. But one thing is clear, unless pulp mills are stringently regulated and are subject to the most rigorous environmental standards, the consequences both in northern Alberta and in the territories right up to the Arctic can be catastrophic.
It is this sort of thing, as well, that I would suggest any new forestry department must take into account as part of its mandate. The effects on the forestry industry are every bit as much an attribute of the forestry industry as are the revenues that that industry can generate. The department must understand that, and the department must incorporate that into its mandate.
There are other things that any such new department must consider. There are questions that generally revolve around the sustainability of forestry as an industry in Canada, questions that incorporate considerations like cutting practices. I am certain many of the members of this House who have had the opportunity to drive the beautiful mountain highways of Alberta and British Columbia during our delightful summer months have seen the incredibly panoramic vistas before them as they drive those highways, and have noted huge sides of
mountains stripped of trees, indeed, of virtually all vegetation rising more than a foot or so above the surface. This is clear cutting, and it is an environmentally hazardous practice, especially in sensitive watersheds. Yet clear cutting remains the dominant-to use the industry's term-harvesting technique in Canadian forestry. This is an especially difficult problem in Alberta because ours are poor grey-wooded soils where the main forest harvest is to occur, and those soils are especially sensitive to the impact of clear cutting.
Among the things this department must do, Mr. Speaker, is examine and indeed facilitate and foster alternatives to clear cutting. We must look at the diversification of those products that we take from our forests. There is a vast range of products that now can be created from forestry, not just board lumber and not just pulp and paper. The department's mandate should include efforts, in current vernacular, to "sus out" those alternatives and popularize them.
Finally, it should be noted that in our urban areas we already have forests of paper merely waiting to be recycled. And that, too, is a legitimate concern of the forestry department.
New Democrats do support this bill. We support the creation of a department of forestry and have done so for many years. But the Bill does not go quite far enough. The forestry department, as envisioned in this bill, is not quite sufficiently effective. There are changes that must be made and which are perfectly worthy of study by the Standing Committee.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: We will have the question and comment period, after Question Period. It being 11 o'clock, we will now proceed with Statements by Members.

Mr. Speaker, on October 25, in Costa Rica at a meeting of the countries of the western hemisphere, Prime Minister Brian Mulroney is expected to make an announcement

that will forever change the face of Canadian foreign policy with respect to Latin America. For decades now, countries such as Mexico and the Caribbean Islands, who are members of the Organization of American States, have asked Canada to join in the hope that their concerns would be better represented than they are by the government in Washington. Canada has steadfastly refused, as the Organization has been perceived as merely an extension of American foreign policy and our membership in it may serve to compromise our independence regarding our own relationship with member countries.
Growing Canadian trade and a trend towards democracy may, indeed, be good reasons to re-evaluate our past positions. Any re-evaluation, however, should be done in consultation with Canadian groups and agencies across Canada who work very closely with member countries and therefore would have invaluable input into the final decisions. This is a very important change in the direction for our country.
I urge the Prime Minister to seriously consider not making a decision on this issue until we are able, possibly in the External Affairs Committee, to study whether it is in our interests and whether it is in the interests of member countries for us to join the OAS.

Mr. Speaker, after having recently spent some time in the Soviet Union and particularly in Ukraine, I was able to observe the positive developments of Mr. Gorbachev's policies of perestroika and glasnost. There is now a window of opportunity to show Canadian support for those changes taking place in the Soviet Union.
At the present time, Canadian businessmen are travelling in Ukraine and are considering joint ventures in Ukrainian enterprises. Therefore, on the occasion of the Prime Minister's visit to the Soviet Union and Ukraine, I strongly encourage him to take that opportunity to
announce the opening of a Canadian consulate in Kiev, the capital of Ukraine. This would follow an earlier decision of West Germany to do so. The Canadian counsulate would facilitate tourism and cultural and economic exchanges with that part of the Soviet Union and would show support for Mr. Gorbachev's policies.

Mr. Speaker, this week, for reasons known only to themselves, the Canadian Auto Workers, through some representatives, have garnered considerable publicity in Nova Scotia with threats to block National Sea Products trucks from exporting unprocessed fish from Nova Scotia.
Export trade, particularly to the United States, is the backbone of the Atlantic fishery. If Canada wishes to participate in trade with GATT nations, like it or lump it, Canada must abide by GATT rules.
If the CAW can write a law or a regulation that would prevent the export of unprocessed fish from Nova Scotia and is GATT consistent, then I and many others would welcome it. Such activity would be far more helpful to the people of Lockport than irresponsible actions which can only serve to scare off potential investors from CAW plants.

Mr. Speaker, I rise today to draw the attention of the House to the crisis in the Republic of Armenia in the Soviet Union, crisis caused by the almost total blockade imposed by its neighbour, the Republic of Azerbaijan.
Almost all supplies in Armenia must pass through Azerbaijan. Because of this blockade, industry is paralysed, oil has run out, rebuilding from the earthquake is coming to a halt, and food and other necessities are in increasingly short supply.



This reprehensible blockade stems from the persistent dispute over control of the Ngomo-Karabagh region. The population of Ngomo-Karabagh is comprised predominantly of ethnic Armenians and they have expressed their desire and determination to be reunited with Soviet Armenia.
The U.S.S.R. Government has been at best ineffective in resolving this dispute. We implore it to act quickly to end the blockade of Armenia and to work for a solution which will ensure the security and respect the fundamental rights of the Armenian people. We strongly encourage Mr. Gorbachev to talk seriously with representatives of the Ngomo-Karabagh regarding their demand for reunification with their Armenian homeland.

Mr. Speaker, I am pleased to point out in the House today that thanks to the economic policies of our Government and the cooperation that now exists with the provincial Government, the region of Sept-Iles in my riding was selected as the site for an aluminum smelter. This project, which involves a private investment of $1.3 billion, will create nearly 2,000 construction jobs and provide permanent employment for almost 700 workers.
The Alouette Inc. aluminum project^ came about because of the determination of the Sept-Iles community, the willingness of German, Austrian, Dutch, Japanese and Quebec investors and the participation of the federal Government in developing port facilities.
Mr. Speaker, that is a fine example of cooperation between the federal and provincial governments and private capital which is giving my region an unprecedented economic boost!

subtopic: WITHDRAWAL OF VIETNAMESE TROOPS FROM CAMBODIA
WITHDRAWAL OF VIETNAMESE TROOPS FROM CAMBODIA
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, as preoccupied as we have been in Parliament in the last week with rising taxes and disappearing trains, it is important for members of Parliament to raise their heads and pause for a moment at greater tragedies happening around the world. This morning I would like to point in particular to the withdrawal this week of Vietnamese troops from Cambodia without any ceasefire or internal settlement, leaving the fear and the potential crisis of a new civil war emerging in that tragic country.
Canadians will remember the horrifying reports of the killing of over a million people at the hands of the Khmer Rouge just a few short years ago. With the coming of the dry season, the potential of a new civil war emerging looms large.
For our part, Canada has been invited to act as a member of an observer team, and while western nations have been reluctant to join in without a comprehensive agreement, it does not mean we should stand idly by without making some real effort to find a resolution to the tragic conflict.
We hope that at the meetings this week in the General Assembly of the United Nations, the Secretary of State for External Affairs will use the good offices of this country to remind western nations of our responsibility and will do everything we can to avoid another conflict in that tragic but very lovely country.

Mr. Speaker, I think it is important for the House to recognize on the last sitting day of September that this month has been declared to be Child Abuse Prevention Month by the Independent Order of Foresters, IOF.
During September, the IOF has undertaken an awareness raising effort in communities across Canada in order to diminish the problem of child abuse. Child abuse, like other forms of family violence, is an issue of grave concern, not only to the federal government but
September 29, 1989

to all Canadians. Prevention of this horrible crime is our ultimate goal. The goal can only be realized through the concerted efforts of many partners, including the federal government, the provinces, the territories, community groups, professionals in the field and, most important, aware and informed parents.
The Independent Order of Foresters is to be commended for its efforts this month in helping the public recognize the problem of child abuse and for offering positive steps toward solving it.

Mr. Speaker, lives will be lost and time wasted if the federal government goes ahead with plans to shut down search and rescue operations at Canadian Forces Base Summerside. Two retired senior officers of the Canadian Armed Forces have told us this.
Lieutenant Colonel Dennis Hopping, who commanded the search and rescue squadron from 1981 to 1984, said the move from Prince Edward Island makes no sense from an operational point of view. Major Gary Naylor, who was commander of the rescue co-ordination centre in Halifax, said he expressed similar concerns in a letter to the Minister of National Defence last spring and received no reply.
Both men pointed to a major report on defence tabled in 1982 which identifies Summerside as the optimum site for search and rescue operations in Atlantic Canada, an opinion the federal government appeared to support until last spring. We know that in April the federal government announced its intention to close the base and to move search and rescue out of Summerside. This is a crippling blow to Summerside, wiping out 2,900 jobs.
A time when the fishery on the east coast is in crisis, a time when the social security net, the unemployment insurance, is being dismantled by this government, is no time to play with the lives of fishermen and mariners in the north Atlantic. I call on the Government of Canada to do the sensible thing, the wise thing, to restore search and rescue to P.E.I. and give the people back their jobs.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Transport
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, it is with much regret that I inform the House of yet another instance when our national parole system has failed us. In the 1960s Blaire Donald Johnson was convicted of murder with malice in the United States. Again in 1980, this time in Canada, he was convicted of rape.
In August of this year he was released on full parole. Less than one month has passed since the approval of his full release and he has struck again. Six days ago in my B.C. riding of Fraser Valley East he was charged with unlawful confinement and sexual assault.
Clearly we live in a dangerous world which warrants strong measures in order to protect the public. In this case, the current system has failed. How was it that a twice convicted violent criminal was allowed out on our streets? How was it that the current system allowed this man to slip through? The parole board cannot be easily perfected, but perhaps at this time its parole procedures could be re-evaluated. Therefore, I call upon the Solicitor General to look into this matter and put an end to such preventable crimes in the future.

Mr. Speaker, the public hearings on Bill C-21, which changes the Unemployment Insurance Act, have been concluded. There has emerged from these hearings one common theme expressed by cities, community groups, national organizations and private citizens alike in reaction to these changes and that is one of anger.
The government's claim that it was introducing these changes in order to make unemployment insurance fair has been shown for what it really is, an attempt to punish the victims of the system. Time after time, government members of the committee referred to polls showing that Canadians think unemployment insurance is abused, in spite of the minister's statement that abuse was not an issue.

There is an abuser of the unemployment insurance system and it is the government through this act. Increasing the qualifying period is an abuse of the victims of the government's failed economic policies. Decreasing the length of benefit periods is an abuse of the victims of the government's failed right-wing agenda. Doubling the penalty for women who have to quit their jobs because of sexual harassment or because they have to meet the needs of their children is an abuse of Canadian women.
Canadians have told the government in no uncertain terms that these changes to the unemployment insurance system are immoral.

Mr. Speaker, I am happy to see that, thanks to the Canada-United States Free Trade Agreement, Ontario-based Arriscraft Corporation has decided to build an ultra-modem plant in Quebec rather than in New England.
Next spring Arriscraft will build in Saint-Etienne-des-Gres in my riding of Saint-Maurice a $12 million calcium silicate brick factory.
That decision to choose Quebec over the United States shows once again this Government's economic foresight.

From the great city of Cambridge, Ontario to St-Etienne-des-Gres in my riding, Arriscraft Corporation will now be able to compete in the north American market and also succeed.

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I would like to draw the attention of the House to a serious matter directly affecting the health of thousands of Canadians in southwestern Ontario. The Great Lakes Water Quality Board says that river and lake bottom sediments are huge reservoirs of pollutants. Now the government is dredging up these materials from the St. Clair River and dumping them in 15 feet of water in Lake St. Clair.
Today the Walpole Island First Nation announced that it is seeking an injunction requiring the federal government to cease all dredging of these potentially hazardous materials from the bottom of the St. Clair River until a full environmental assessment is completed. This project has been undertaken without an environmental impact study and without consulting the Walpole Island Nation whose people rely on the river and lake for their traditional economy.
I and the Member for Kent ask the government to stop this dredging unless and until a full environmental assessment shows it is safe to do so. I and the Member for Kent ask the government to show more concern for the health and safety of the thousands of Canadians living in the vicinity of the St. Clair River and Lake St. Clair.

Mr. Albert Cooper (Peace River) Mr. Speaker, Canada is a very special nation, a country blessed with abundance, a land filled with resources. We are a country envied around the world, an envy that has attracted people to our land and allowed us to build a nation that provides opportunity to our citizens and dreams for our youth.
This is not a country that anyone should take for granted or treat as the stakes for a game of Russian roulette. Canada is a country worth fighting for. I call on our premiers to reach out to one another in generosity and in kindness to achieve agreement on the Meech Lake Accord, to take our nation through this first round of constitutional reform and to lead our country into maturity.
Now is the time to set aside our personal and political differences and to follow the example of the Hon. Member for Shefford.

Mr. Speaker, Canadians concerned about the environment were extremely unhappy with the decision taken by the Minister of the Environment to proceed with the Rafferty-Alameda project without holding a public environmental impact assessment and were similarly disgusted with the bungled attempt to export Canadian PCBs across the world.

Despite the public promises of the Conservatives to take environmental consequences into account in making all economic decision, we see the Minister of Finance promoting the GST without any concern whatsoever for the negative environmental consequences. Why should environmentally friendly goods be taxed at the same rate as goods and services which poison our air and drinking water and contribute to our monumental waste disposal problems?
The Minister of the Environment should hang his head for supporting a regressive tax regime which taxes recycled paper at the same rate as other paper, bicycles at the same rate as cars, alternate energy at the same rate as fossil fuels which contribute to the greenhouse effect, cloth diapers at the same rate as disposable ones.
Jim MacNeil, Secretary General of the Brundtland Commission, was dead on yesterday for condemning the Conservative government for being long on talk and short on action for protecting our environment. It is time for green taxes, not grief taxes.

speakerposition: Deputy Whip of the Liberal Party

Mr. Speaker, I rise today to impress upon the government the need for close scrutiny at Canada Post. The London Free Press today, has a front page story which alleges that managers at Canada Post in London, Ontario, have been artificially doctoring employee attendance records to make employees who were absent appear as though they had been present. One has to wonder why these kinds of activities are going on and why it is that someone would have the motivation to do so if those allegations are in fact correct.
I have in hand an internal letter of Canada Post dated February 7, 1986, in which one manager brings the following to the attention of lower managers. He says:
Any raises for MPS categories are hinged directly to our control of absenteeism. Last year I got no raise! This year I want one! Do your part, it is all that I ask.
We have suspected for some time that there are bonuses at Canada Post for managers who twist the arms
Oral Questions
of people below them. This seems to be proof of exactly that kind of practice.

Mr. Speaker, in the absence of the Prime Minister, I will put my question to the Deputy Prime Minister. Canadians learned today that the decision concerning VIA Rail was not taken as a result of the government's budget-cutting exercise as we were led to believe. I have learned that it was discussed on November 22, one day after the federal election, according to a leading newspaper.
This is an attempt to fool Canadians. I ask the Deputy Prime Minister, why did the government try to mislead Canadians on this very important question?

Mr. Speaker, I would like to see a little more consistency on that side of the House of Commons. Yesterday I was accused of not being aware of what happened to transport in the April budget and that everything had been imposed on me.
Tbday the member stated that there was a document which was issued in November saying that I proposed to cut VIA Rail. I believe that he should make up his mind as to whether it is November or April. Please, I do not think we need two versions.

Mr. Speaker, I did not say that to the minister because I did not put my question to the minister. Again, since it was the Deputy Prime Minister who reinstated routes that had been cancelled previously and told people to "use it or lose it", I would ask the Deputy Prime Minister why the government is refusing to consider all the facts before taking such Draconian action against the travelling public of this country.

Mr. Speaker, since April and even before then, the Government has been considering various factors to determine the future of VIA Rail.

September 29, 1989
Oral Questions
I said not long ago, in fact I have been saying this all week, that we were involved in a decision-making process and that as soon as the decision is announced, Hon. Members will be able to stop relying on leaked documents at a rate of several per week, and use official documents provided by the Department of Transport.
Mr. Speaker, nothing would enhance the Department of Transport as much as the minister leaving it.
Oh, oh!

I would like to put a question to the Deputy Prime Minister. I would like to ask him if he would consult with the Prime Minister and advise him that the transport committee will be meeting at 9.30 on Tuesday, October 3, and would he ask the Prime Minister to come before that committee and try, if he can, to explain why the government is taking this Draconian action which is going to hurt the Canadian environment, is going to devastate the travelling public and is going to wind up destroying VIA Rail.

Mr. Speaker, I will be very brief. I hope that the committee will do the same work that it did in 1981 when this member was chairman of the Standing Committee on Transport and he cut VIA Rail by 20 per cent.

Mr. Speaker, in the absence of the Prime Minister, my question is directed to the Deputy Prime Minister. Yesterday the government was rushing to defend itself against the charge contained in the RCMP DEA report which was made public yesterday that the government has let Canada become a haven for the proceeds of crime.
After declaring a war on drugs, the government rejected the essential bank deposit reporting requirement which I brought forward when the bill was before the committee. It sat on the bill for six months after it was passed before proclaiming it. Rod Stanler, the distinguished RCMP drug officer, left the force, saying that the government was afraid the new law, and the
Minister of Justice himself yesterday said that because of failings in the law, the municipal police forces of the country are not using it. Instead of declaring itself a success, why does the government not admit that this law is a failure and bring forward amendments to correct it?

Mr. Speaker, I think it is quite clear that this government has taken very seriously the whole question of money laundering, also the whole question of the problem of drugs as has been indicated by the Prime Minister for a number of years now at a time when he was ridiculed by the members opposite because of the words that he used to describe the problems of drugs in this country.
On the question of money laundering, we have always taken this as a serious matter. We had this report which I should point out is a year out of date. It is a September 1988 report. Since then, we have had Bill C-61 which deals with the proceeds of crime. We have also entered into mutual legal assistance treaties with the United States and other countries.
At the last summit we agreed with our partners in the summit countries to work co-operatively on an international basis to deal with this problem.
In addition to that, the RCMP and ourselves are working very closely with the chartered banks to ensure that the practices that they are following are consistent with what is required to address this problem which is clearly an international problem.
Mr. Kaplan I do not think the Minister knows what is happening. He just said that we entered into a mutual legal assistance treaty. In fact, we endorsed it on our side, but is it not a fact that the U.S. Senate is refusing to ratify that treaty, particularly because Canada has no minimum deposit reporting requirement in our law? That is a report from the Financial Post just the other day.
I want to ask the Minister to retract the statement that we have a mutual legal assistance treaty. In fact, we do not, and we will not have one until we have a proper law in this country about the proceeds of crime.
Mr. Speaker, the Member is quite correct that we have indicated our readiness to ratify that mutual assistance treaty.
That's not what you said, Mike.

I just said that I agreed with the member opposite. We have not had the United States saying to us that they are ready to ratify that treaty. We have been working closely with it, though, in an operational sense, and we will continue to work closely as has been indicated by representatives of the Drug Enforcement Agency in the United States on television this morning.
Mr. Speaker, my question is addressed to the Minister of Transport.
Hear, hear!

Perhaps he will stop his clapping when he hears the question.
The Government of Canada, through the office of the Prime Minister during the election campaign in 1988 promised to improve VIA Rail. This was during the election campaign, I repeat. We now learn, according to a report in today's press, that while this promise was being made, the government had already made a decision for major cut-backs in VIA Rail and the then President of VIA Rail was informed of that but had been asked to keep quiet during that election period. Why was the Government of Canada saying one thing during the election campaign while simultaneously making its decision about VIA Rail to go in the opposite direction?

Mr. Speaker, I will not stop clapping. It was not because the member asked me a question. It was because I appreciate the reason why his party was applauding and I will continue to clap.
Now, concerning VIA Rail, first of all the document that the leader of the NDP is referring to is a document that I have not seen. It seems to be a leaked document, but even if the document has been leaked, the document referred to November 22, the day when I was at my doctor's office for surgery I would undergo the week after. I was surely not deciding about VIA Rail.

Mr. Speaker, the minister's medical appointments to one side, whether it was on that precise day or not, the accusation is extremely serious. The accusation is made that the head of VIA Rail knew that a
Oral Questions
decision had been made to have cuts in VIA Rail but had been asked to keep quiet during that period, and at the same time the Prime Minister's Office, in response to questions about government proposals for action on VIA Rail during the election, was promising, to quote the document put out by the Prime Minister's Office, to enhance the service of VIA Rail.
Was the president of VIA or was he not informed at that time of a decision that had been taken? Why, I repeat, was the Government of Canada, in an election campaign, saying one thing about VIA Rail and at the same time planning to go in the opposite direction?

Mr. Speaker, obviously a process is now in place for the decision making on cutbacks at VIA Rail, and this process ended or started, as the case may be, on April 27, the budget cuts were announced. Almost six months after the election campaign, the Budget was brought down in which the Government announced its intention to cut back on spending. I think this is a completely normal process. I intervened in the process when I had to, contrary to what was said yesterday. I repeat, what is important is that the corporation had to be given spending levels commensurate with our ability to pay, and this was made clear in the April Budget, but I repeat, this was part of a procedure that took several months to establish.

Mr. Speaker, the Minister did not answer the question. My last question is as follows: The Minister responsible for Montreal said yesterday that he did not know what impact these cuts would have on the Montreal area. However, according to recent information, we are going to lose 3,800 jobs in Montreal, 500 in Winnipeg, 300 in Halifax, which means a total of 13,000 jobs in Canada. My question for the Minister is very direct: Will he publicly admit today that the Government intends to abolish 13,000 jobs?

Mr. Speaker, of course I will not confirm those figures which, once again, are based on documents that are not official. I have no idea where those figures come from because I have not seen them, and so I see it is my responsibility, Mr. Speaker, not to confirm either the document or the figures it contains.

Oral Questions

Mr. Speaker, on Wednesday the Minister of Transport said in this House, and I quote:
The Minister of Finance has decided for the best of this country to
determine new reference levels for VIA Rail.
This is the first time that we have an admission by the Minister of Transport that the decisions on VIA Rail were in fact made by the Minister of Finance. What the Minister of Finance and his department know about transportation policy in this country is beyond me.
Let me address my question to the Minister of Finance. When will he table in this House the studies and criteria used by his department to determine those reference levels? We need the supporting documentation on how he arrived at these figures and perhaps the minister will be kind enough to tell us when this information will be brought to the House.

Mr. Speaker, I said yesterday and I repeat it today, as I just said to the Leader of the NDP, I have been a part of this decision all along.
Yesterday I was accused of not being part of the process and today your colleague said that I did in November. I think, once again, we need a little consistency. The possible cuts at VIA Rail, the cuts in the reference levels, have been decided by the cabinet.

Mr. Speaker, I agree with the minister that we need a little consistency and let me just clarify some information that has been coming forward.
VIA Rail in fact does use 3 per cent of those people using transportation needs in our country. But in context, the bus service in this country uses 4 per cent, the air services use 7 per cent and the automobiles on the highways use 86 per cent. So in context 3 per cent is a rather large number.
Having said that, my next question is to the Minister of Finance also. The $250 million used in your statistic, 1993, is calculated in 1993 terms. Does the Minister of Finance say that this in effect destroys passenger rail service in this country?

Mr. Speaker, I believe that the reference levels were determined based on the capacity of Canadians to pay for the budget as a whole. The member gave a few figures, he said 3, 4, 5, 6 per
cent, and I think those figures are accurate, but at the same time the Department of Transport has to determine subsidies or support for different kinds of transportation modes.
We have determined that VIA Rail, transporting just 3 per cent of intercity passengers, should be cut in light of the fact that in terms of the reference we had for the other modes of transport, VIA Rail was over-subsidized. This is the reason why we have those figures.

Mr. Speaker, my question is to the Minister of Finance. Because the threshold of the GST tax credit system is not fully indexed, over half a million low-income Canadian families who would be eligible for full refundable GST credits in 1991 will lose either part or all of their credits within five years. Because of this erosion, within 10 years over one million will lose their credits.
Can the minister explain why he has decided not to protect low-income Canadians?

Mr. Speaker, I think it is quite clear that the government has been sensitive to the impacts of the indexation formula that is now in the tax system, the CPI minus three formula. As an example, on the question of the refundable sales tax credit, we started with a threshold of $15,000, then we moved it up to $16,000, then we moved it to $18,000. Now with the GST proposal it is going to be $25,000.
That indicates that we review these programs on an ongoing basis and we make adjustments where they are appropriate. I think it would be wrong for the hon. member to draw the conclusions, as he has, that in a certain period of time X thousand people will be ineligible for the GST credit. All elements of the tax system are indexed the same way and all elements of the tax system will continue to be indexed the same way. They will be adjusted as appropriate as time goes by.

Mr. Speaker, obviously where these credits are not fully indexed, year by year, each year and every year, Canadians lose the value of that credit system. Obviously this tax must be withdrawn. If the minister is really serious about protecting low-income Canadians from this regressive GST he will not increase the burden placed on these people.
September 29, 1989

Will the minister commit to the House today to fully index the income thresholds of the tax credits and the tax credit system in order to protect all low-income Canadians?

Mr. Speaker, I think fair-minded Canadians would see clearly that what we are doing in the GST tax system is changing from the regressive nature of the sales tax system we inherited in 1984 whereby people who were in low-income brackets were paying 2 or 3 percentage points more of their income in sales tax than those in upper incomes. That is clearly regressive.
With the refundable sales tax credit and the GST credit that we are bringing with the GST tax system, we have changed that so that people in low incomes will be paying 2 or 3 percentage points less of their income than those in upper-income brackets. Mr. Speaker, I said yesterday what I think about the kind of figures my friend is proposing. If it is working so well, if people are using the train that much, how can we have those figures where we have deficits of more than $600 million?

Mr. Speaker, the document I have is not a fabrication. It is a document which was produced by VIA Rail and submitted to its board of directors earlier this month. What this document shows, Mr. Speaker, is that in spite of the antiquated equipment and the very poor marketing that VIA has been able to do because of the cuts, more and more people are using the train, and we have to find a way to invest in rail passenger services so that more people can use it and we can lower the cost, because it is possible.

Mr. Speaker, I know that the NDP always has the magical formula. We know that, everybody knows that. But he didn't give any figures about costs. Last year, 1988, revenues were up $26 million, but expenditures were $94 million more. Is this the kind of management he wants?
