The House resumed consideration of the motion of Mr. Mulroney that Bill C-29, an Act to establish the Department of Forestry, to amend the Forestry Development and Research Act and to make related amendments to other Acts, be read the second time and referred to a legislative committee.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: We shall now proceed to questions and comments following the speech by the Hon. Member for Edmonton East (Mr. Harvey). The Hon. Member for Champlain (Mr. Champagne), on questions and comments.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of State (Forestry)
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I listened very carefully to what my NDP colleague from Edmonton East (Mr. Harvey) had to say. I have two comments on his speech. My first one is that the Hon. Member raised the possibility of referring the Bill to the Standing Committee. Mr. Speaker, the Government decided to refer the Bill to a legislative committee because obsious-ly the Government wants to observe the spirit of the McGrath reform. As you know, this reform makes it possible for Members to go to the legislative committee and consider the specific of a bill.
Second, Mr. Speaker, the legislative committee will consist only of individuals who are specifically interested in forestry. This is important because the Standing Committee covers both forestry and fisheries. We agreed that it would be better in this particular case to go to the legislative committee.
Mr. Speaker, the Hon. Member and several other Opposition Members mentioned figures that appear in the Estimates for the current year, saying that the ministry's budget had been cut. I may remind Hon. Members that what they saw in the Estimates of 1989-90 are figures that are incomplete, in that they represent -At this point, as you know, Mr. Speaker, the agreements are about to expire, and generally, the agreements are included in the various budgets. Six agreements out of ten are to be re-negotiated, while the other agreements will expire next year.

It is also a fact that the budgets are always lower when we get to the last year of a series of agreements. I think I should warn the Opposition that these figures does not necessarily reflect what future spending by the Department of Forestry will be and that because we will have a better idea when all the agreements have been renewed.
In concluding, Mr. Speaker, I would like to say that if we consider the Estimates that were tabled last February, it was said that for this year the Department would have a budget of $206 million with 1,226 person-years. Today, and this is the point I am trying to make, we are up to $211 million, with 1,328 person-years, which is more than for 1988-89. Mr. Speaker, I want to make sure all the Members are aware of this fact and are not too hasty in their judgments about the impact of current budgets on the future Department of Forestry.

Mr. Speaker, under questions and comments, I just want to make a few comments.
The parliamentary secretary has made some comments which I think it would be wise for us to put in the proper perspective.
What we are trying to do is help the minister of forestry by giving him a little more authority. We are arguing that we want the minister of forestry to have more authority, more money and more personnel in his department. There is nothing wrong with that. That is what we are in favour of.
The other thing he mentioned is that the agreements have expired and none of that money is in the forestry budget yet and that is why the budget looks a little lower. Let me tell you that the budgets for the forestry agreements are not going to be found in the forestry department. They are going to be under the control of other ministries. That is what we are worried about. We would like to see all of the budget money into the forestry department. There is no doubt about it.
Let me assure you and the hon. parliamentary secretary that we are in favour of a full-fledged forestry department. We are very pleased that we are going to have one. However, we would like it to be much stronger than that. Maybe the member for Edmonton East would like to comment on that aspect as well.
Government Orders

Mr. Speaker, to return to the remarks of the hon. parliamentary secretary, he suggested that the reference of the bill to a legislative committee was' superior in this instance to the reference of the bill to the standing committee because the standing committee includes within its mandate the responsibility for fisheries.
This is, I will grant him, a colourful argument, but I do not know if it is quite to the point. Because the committee's mandate includes fisheries does not require it as a committee to include the question of fisheries in all of the business it does, just as the Standing Committee on Energy, Mines and Resources is quite competent to consider matters dealing only with Canada's energy resources-and, in fact, we did so earlier this week when we had the National Energy Board before us-to the complete exclusion of questions of, for example, mines. I do not recall one single question being put to the NEB regarding mines.
Therefore, it is possible for the Standing Committee on Forestry and Fisheries to, for the purpose of studying this bill, concern itself solely with fisheries. For example, if the Canadian Institute of Forestry was to appear before that committee, I feel very confident in saying that it would be most unlikely that any member of that committee would put to that institute a question regarding fisheries.
The argument that the bill must be referred to the legislative committee as opposed to the standing committee I do not think has yet been unassailably made.
The question of the budget figures, and the contention that the figures are incomplete because we are at the end of a period during which several agreements are expiring, is an interesting rhetorical point to which I will respond. Surely, it is up to the ministry to place before this House estimates of its expenditures as complete as they can possibly make them.
If they are intending to sign agreements this year, and if in consequence of those agreements the ministry is intending to spend money then, by heaven, estimates for that expenditure ought to be included in the budgetary estimates presented to this House. Those estimates are the only documents we have to go on. If they are not including expenditures that they fully expect to undertake in those estimates, then they are to that degree at least misleading this House. I leave that to them.

Government Orders

Mr. Speaker, in response to the points made by the Hon. Member for Edmonton East (Mr. Harvey), I may recall that referring the Bill to the legislative committee will give Members with a special interest in forestry a chance to work on the Bill and thus make a contribution that will be far more useful than if the Bill was referred to the Standing Committee on Forestry and Fisheries.
I may also remind the Hon. Member that I listened carefully to his speech, and that after he mentioned at the beginning of his speech that he felt the Government wanted to expedite passage of the Bill, I was surprised when I heard him say later that he would have preferred to see the Bill referred for consideration to the Standing Committee on Forestry and Fisheries, in order to slow down the process.
I can inform the Hon. Member that my riding, Man-icouagan, has a large number of forestry operations. It is a riding that needs dynamic policies for reforestation, a riding that needs research and development, and I would be very disappointed if the Bill were not given speedy consideration by the legislative committee and the House of Commons.
Throughout his speech, the Hon. Member mentioned a series of factors, events and situations which in my view confirm that this Bill should be passed as soon as possible. He referred to the situation at the paper mills. He mentioned clearcutting and referred to air pollution, acid rain and contaminated effluents.
Mr. Speaker, I think all these factors argue in favour of getting Bill C-29 as quickly as possible through the legislative committee so that it can then be referred back to the House of Commons.

Mr. Speaker, again, I would just briefly note that the government's new found concern for expeditious treatment of this bill is welcome on this side of the assembly. We only ask where they were from 1984 until 1989.
I would say as well that we have no objection to the bill going to the legislative committee on the assumption that that committee will hear witnesses on the bill. We
consider that to be a virtually minimal demand in this regard. So, if you are going to refer it to the legislative committee, fine, go ahead, but please hear witnesses.
Mr. Dave Worthy (Cariboo-Chilcotin: Mr. Speaker, I am pleased to rise to support Bill C-29. In fact, I am very proud to be able to participate in the legislation that will finally create a full department of forestry for Canada. As a Canadian, I applaud this far-sighted legislation. But this legislation is also important to me as a British Columbian. It is no exaggeration to state that it could be vital to the future well-being of both my province as well as Canada.
Forestry, as we know, has been de-emphasized by previous governments. It is an attitude that is strange to me. It is a strange approach to an industry which is the largest in Canada. It is number one in our exports. It is an industry that is in a position to help meet the ever-growing demands for forest products in the world.
Fortunately, Mr. Speaker, the present government has moved decisively to support the forest sector. Now with this bill a full federal forestry department will be created, and will provide national leadership in generating and applying forest and forest resource policies. Its initiatives and programs will support the government's commitment to environmentally sustainable economic development. It will make forestry agreements with individuals, organizations as well as other governments. It will conduct and promote research and development in the forestry sector.
If anyone still wonders about the need for national leadership in the forestry sector, I would like to take a few minutes to just briefly outline the magnitude of the forest products industry in Canada.
Over $40 billion of product is produced by the forest industry. There are over $20 billion worth of exports. As I said earlier, it is the largest exporter in Canada. In fact, Canada is the world's largest exporter of forest products. We see that British Columbia probably produces close to half of the products in lumber. But if you look at the total forest products industry across Canada, you will see that Ontario has 212,000 people working in forestry. Quebec has 230,000 people, more than in British Columbia. In British Columbia we have 216,000 people working in the forest industry. Atlantic Canada which needs the work that the forest industry can provide, currently has
September 29, 1989

66,000 people employed in the forest industry. Across the prairies there are 46,000 people employed.
One thing we have to understand when we talk about forestry in Canada is that very few of our forest lands are, in fact, controlled by the federal government. It is the provinces that control the forest lands. There is a need for this government to provide leadership, but it has to be done in a co-operative manner. It is this government over the last five years that has shown the initiative to initiate that leadership and the mood of co-operation that is essential.
It is far more than what we have done and are doing in terms of jobs. This is an industry for the future. It is for that reason that I feel it is imperative that this new forestry department is in a position to provide the leadership and the co-operative approach to develop our future.
When speaking to this bill everyone in the House has acknowledged this government and its initiation of the FRDA projects across Canada which have been universally acceptable. They are considered by all Canadians to have finally put the emphasis in forestry where it should be. That has been done in co-operation with the provinces.
Many people have said that the FRDA projects are replacing forests that have been taken by industry. That is really not how we have used these FRDA dollars. I would like to emphasize that there are many things that can impact our forest land. There are natural growth stands that are too thick and therefore produce crops that are unhealthy and do not have good trees. We have lands destroyed by forest fires that have not naturally regenerated. In many parts of Canada thousands of acres have been hit with the blight of various diseases that affect our trees. It is these areas of Canada, insufficiently restocked areas of our forest lands, that the FRDA projects have been attacking over the past four years.
It is in fact to the future that we should look with these. We could double the volume of logs now brought in to the forest industry if we properly farm our forests. If we do the thinning, natural fertilizing, and the proper
Government Orders
processing of those forests, we can double the amount of fibre that we take off those lands. We also have the capacity to use the wood that is now considered waste.
For instance, 50 per cent of the wood that is brought into the sawmills is not utilized in forest products per se. It is either burnt or consumed as energy. All that 50 per cent waste is potentially usable fibre, and it is learning how to use that fibre that will create many of the jobs we require in the forest industry.
There are also many new products that this government can help ensure that get past the point of just talking about and that we actually get into the process of producing and exporting.
There is another area I would like to mention. The environmental ramifications of the forest industry have been mentioned by many people. We cannot just log the forests. We have to do it in such a way that it meets the demands that we place on it for proper environmental use. It has to be done so that all the industries that want to share our forest resources are in a position to do so. Meeting that challenge and demand is going to be where this new department of forestry can paste its brightest star on the calendar board.
I know that many have criticized the budget. They say that the budget for the forestry is not sufficient, that we should be putting more money in it. We cannot just throw money at these problems. The Canadian public expects us to do more for less in this government.
We will do well to follow the example of many industries in Canada and the United States which have shown that the pursuit of excellence is possible and that we can in fact address and solve the problems exercising leadership and co-operation. Hopefully we will not have to go to the Canadian people for vast sums of money to achieve that.
In closing, I would like to say that this bill is about our commitment to a vital industry and it is about the commitment to the birthright of our future children.

Mr. Speaker, I would like to congratulate the member on his speech. He is a fellow British Columbian whose riding actually abuts mine. I certainly welcome his contributions.

Government Orders
I have a brief comment and a question or two for the member. The parliamentary secretary earlier in debate today made a comment that I would like some clarification from the member on, if he is able to give clarification. He stated that the legislation has to be passed before we can get on with the renewal of new forest agreements. I do not know if the parliamentary secretary is sure of that comment. As a government member from Cariboo-Chilcotin, perhaps the hon. member can give us some clarification. Clearly that has not been part of the discussion to date on renewed forest agreements. This is certainly the first comment we have heard that this legislation has to pass before any new forest agreements can be approved. It is those forest agreements that I would like to comment on and also ask a question.
The government members opposite and ourselves included have talked about the valuable contribution that these forest agreements have made to reforestation and intensive silviculture in all the provinces. Of course government members have lauded their support of those. We would be interested in their support in renewing these agreements. I remind the members that there are currently three forest agreements with Alberta, Saskatchewan and Manitoba that expired at the end of March, and there are ongoing discussions in B.C. about renewing our forest agreement.
In light of the fact that in the Western Diversification Fund available funds for new federal-provincial agreements have been identified at around $242 million, and in light of the fact that representations by the provinces and others on forestry agreements alone total nearly $400 million, I would like to ask the member if he can give us an idea, because the minister to date certainly has not nor has the finance minister, what the provinces might be able to expect in a renewed forest agreement and other economic agreements when in fact there is such a pittance in the Western Diversification Fund.

Mr. Speaker, I am not privy to any more knowledge than the member for Prince George on the subject of FRDA. I know that they are in process. I personally feel that the formation of the full forestry department which will elevate the current Minister of State to full minister status will in fact put him in a position to influence from within the federal government and in that new position to have more impact with provincial forestry counterparts.
The expedient passage of this current bill and the formation of the full department will be a very positive step toward the new FRDAs. I really do appreciate that the member from Prince George is fully on board the train that was started by the Conservatives on these agreements.
I have heard him many times speak strongly for the FRDA programs that we now have and how essential the new ones will be. We do appreciate his support. It is continuing to be high priority on the government agenda, and I can assure the member that it is of extremely high priority on this member's agenda.

Mr. Speaker, my question deals very specifically with what is a blight on B.C.'s economic horizon, that is the fact that on an ongoing basis raw logs are being exported with no value added.
Raw logs have been exported from the coast of British Columbia in the following manner: in 1984, 12 per cent of the lumber output was raw logs with no value added; in 1985 it was almost 9 per cent; in 1986 it was almost 10 per cent; in 1987 it was 10 per cent; and in 1988 it was 9 per cent. Of course the member knows that exporting raw logs is exporting jobs from Canada.
I would like to know what specific provisions the new forestry minister will undertake to stop this blatant export of Canadian jobs at the expense of Canadian foresters.

I can't speak for the minister, Mr. Speaker, nor will I attempt to, but I can explain a little about the export of raw logs which I do not support, either, under most circumstances.
There was very little exporting of logs from the Pacific coast until we hit the severe recession in the 1980s. At that time many of the loggers up the coast had no market for their logs. At that point the provincial government expanded on the permits to export.
Unfortunately those exports continued for some time. There have been many representations by myself as an individual, from some people in the industry, from the unions, and Jack Munro, the president of IWA, to that very point over the past year. In fact, the provincial government has made changes to its exporting. The exporting of those logs is being wound down and now only special circumstance type logs that we cannot take advantage of in our markets will be exported in the years to come.
September 29, 1989

Mr. Speaker, in rising today to speak on Bill C-29, the organization bill for a new forestry department in Canada, I must say that I am always appalled by the government doing something such as this, which is a tremendous idea that we support but putting no money where its mouth is to do the job. To do something without a financial commitment on the part of the government is wrong.
This government can put money into a new forestry department and it is not throwing money to the winds, because we all know that with forestry being such a tremendously important industry to Canada that all Canadians will get their money back in the returns in future years.
If we do not have that commitment today to rebuild, to grow greater forests in this country, to replant lands that should never have been deforested in the first place, if we do not move out there and lay the groundwork for this tremendous industry in the next decades of Canadian economic life, then we are not going to have a solid a forestry business.
The lack of financial commitment to produce something that is going to bring great financial returns in the future is the wrong philosophy. I have heard members of the Conservative Party in this debate give us this age old slogan that they try to peddle across this country: "This government must do more with less".
The Canadian people out there are fully cognizant that this government's real idea is to do less for more. That is the whole scenario behind their tax grab and everything else that goes on around here. This business of telling the people of Canada that the government is going to do more with less is as phoney as a $3 bill. They are in fact doing less for more.
To give you an idea of what they are doing by way of less, Mr. Speaker, all we have to do is point to the devastation that the Minister for International Trade in 1986 did to the softwood lumber industry in this country. She signed the memorandum of understanding that allowed 15 per cent export tax to go on softwood lumber from this country into the United States.
Why did she do that? Members of the northern Ontario caucus, for one group, led by my distinguished
Government Orders
seat-mate from Algoma, can certainly tell you what it meant. We travelled from sawmill to sawmill, from town to town, in northern Ontario in the month of February. Everywhere we went, industry and labour alike in small community Ontario were telling us that the Conservative government sold the softwood lumber industry down the drain in order to get their international free trade agreement.
It is true, because immediately after they signed the memorandum of understanding slapping the 15 per cent tax on softwood lumber going into the U.S., the U.S. signed because it wanted to protect its own manufacturers in the United States.
Can you imagine, Mr. Speaker, a government of Canada going around raving and saying what a great job we have done to sign a free trade agreement when in fact what we have is protectionism, protectionism by the United States, protectionism that was bought by the Conservative government on that late day of 1986 when it sold the softwood lumber industry down the drain and then the U.S. came forward and signed the free trade agreement after its own industry had been protected? Protectionism, Mr. Speaker, is not something you talk about in the same tone, in the same operation as you talk about free trade. Never. They are two absolutely opposite subjects.
Since then under this protection the Conservative government calls free trade the Americans have improved their sawmills. They go to the banks and get loans and they improve their manufacturing processes. Now they are filling the markets that have been traditionally filled by Canadian business over the years.
You can drive anywhere, Mr. Speaker, around the province of Ontario today and you see lumberyards filled more so than I have ever seen in all the years I have been in this House or when I was growing up in a rural area. It is there. It is a fact of life. People are being laid off, so let's not talk about this great positive thing that they are doing for the lumber industry in this country.
Yes, Mr. Speaker, we support the establishment of a forestry department in Canada, but we support one that is going to have some clout. This minister is not going to have any clout under this bill because he has to go to other ministers in cabinet to beg for his finances.

September 29, 1989
Government Orders
It is good to have our excellent forestry research institutions under this departmental roof. I know they are going to be very happy with that.
If we are going to make use of the tremendously positive work, the work that is being done for the future of this country by our forestry research institutions across Canada, then we have to do something out in the field to complement it. We have to grow trees. We have to have an over-all plan. This government has no plan whatsoever.
The first thing that should happen is a federal-provincial meeting of forestry and natural resources ministers across this country with the minister of forestry and the minister should have something to bargain with. He should not have to go to them with hat in hand when he is discussing the future of an important industry in this country. It is not as if we are putting money into something where there will not be any returns. If this government is so gung-ho about great private enterprise in this country, which it has echoed time and time again, why does it not put its money where its mouth is and have a plan to build up the forests in this country and do something?
We have here a very good statement from the Canadian Institute of Forestry, and this has been discussed on the floor of the House before. The Canadian Institute of Forestry would like the new department to have a clearly stated national responsibility, and that responsibility is not clearly stated. It does not have it. The institute wants federal leadership in forestry matters, research and technology transfer, forest resource development, federal-provincial agreements, forest resource data, industry marketing, trade and economics, international forestry- and I mentioned how important international forestry is-human resource, important employment and education programs, and public awareness.
The act should make provision for an interdepartmental committee on forestry so that Forestry Canada can provide federal leadership in the forestry sector. An interdepartmental committee is not new. We have had that before. Consideration should be given to the inclusion of parks, wildlife, lands, waters, surveying, mapping and management of federal forest lands within the mandate of the department. Those are just some of the ideas expressed for this bill.
I want to leave a very positive suggestion in closing my speech. There has to be co-ordination on the jurisdiction of natural resources in this country. I think this is going to be the grounds for a major constitutional discussion at the federal-provincial level in years to come, if we are going to have real co-ordination.
We have several counties in eastern Ontario: Renfrew, Hastings, Lanark, Frontenac, Victoria-Haliburton, Muskoka, Nipissing and others. This is one area where we could have a major reforestation program in these areas where trees must be grown. There is a great expanse of tremendous resource across northern Ontario where people depend upon it for their one community livelihoods. It is a matter of everyday bread and butter. That is the case in many small towns in eastern Ontario as well. So we have a great deal in common here, Mr. Speaker.
There is absolutely no reason why this federal minister cannot sit down with the provincial minister of natural resources and draw up a major plan that will plant trees across this province and across the country.
All this is very, very important to lay the groundwork for it and to show that we are serious about replanting lands that should be left in forestry to show that we are serious working with industry to replant trees that are cut. They will co-operate with on this because it is their future too.

speechtext: The hon. member's time has expired. Questions and comments.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of State (Forestry)
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I listened to my colleague's speech with interest. He is concerned primarily about Canada's forestry polity. I would remind him that since 1984, our Government has emphasized silviculture in a remarkable way by increasing its budget over 300 per cent; this should reassure him. His province, Ontario, has been the main beneficiary.
September 29, 1989

Secondly, he was also concerned about what the Department's mandate might be. I would say it is to provide national leadership in terms of policy. I would reassure him, Mr. Speaker, that the new Department's mandate is to develop and coordinate forestry policies and programs at the national level, to do forestry research and development and encourage it as well, and to work closely with industry and the provincial and territorial agencies concerned in various areas related to the use and protection of forests.
Also, Mr. Speaker, the new Department will work closely with the other federal Departments interested in forests, including Environment Canada, External Affairs and the Department of Regional Industrial Expansion and Science and Technology.
In summary, Mr. Speaker, I think that this legislation is first and foremost intended to make this new Forestry Department a full-fledged department with a minister who will have a free hand to negotiate with the provinces and the other departments concerned for the enhancement of forestry, as we did throughout our last term in office and as we are prepared to do now with the new mandate.

Mr. Hopkins Mr. Speaker, I would like to point out that the work on silviculture that the hon. member mentioned is nothing new. That too has been going on for years in the very capable hands of the excellent research establishments that we have across this country.
I note too that you mention that the department's mandate would have the co-ordination of forestry programs. That is clearly understood. That is nothing new either. You say that they will work closely with other departments. I would hope so. They are going to have to depend on other departments for their financing because the government has failed to give the new department its own financing.
I would also like to ask the hon. member whether or not the present Conservative government will renegotiate the memorandum of understanding on softwood lumber that the Minister for International Trade signed on New Year's Eve of 1986. Will you go back to the drawing board, sit down with the United States, and negotiate your way out of that 15 per cent penalty that you have put on the softwood lumber industry in Canada?
Government Orders
That was a devastating move. It is still having its effect, because not only do they have to contend with paying 15 per cent tax to export the lumber to the U.S., but they also have to contend with higher interest rates in Canada, and there is no indication that they are going to go down, particularly with the introduction by this government of a 9 per cent sales tax that is inflationary.
At the time that that memorandum of understanding was signed in late 1986, the Canadian dollar was at about 71 cents exchange with the American currency, and today it is at about 83 cents, so the lumber industry has lost another 12 per cent right there on the exchange rates alone. What about the spokes in the wheel of progress? You are certainly going to clean the spokes out of the wheel. There is no question about that. I just wonder whether the government is prepared to sit down and negotiate its way out of that 15 per cent penalty that it put on the softwood lumber industry in Canada vis-a-vis the United States in order that the United States would then turn around and sign a free trade agreement and make the softwood lumber industry the goat of the free trade industry.

Mr. Speaker, this summer I had a rare privilege and one which unfortunately is not accessible to every Canadian. I had an opportunity as a city person-my idea of a forest was a walk through Gage Park-to visit northern and western Canada through northern Alberta, the Northwest Territories and British Columbia and had a chance to see, first-hand, some of the beauty of our land and also to begin to understand the challenge that will face any government and any ministry of forestry.
I would like to begin by pointing out the basic concern that I have about this particular bill. First, we are calling it a ministry for forestry. Forestry implies that the function of the forest is to be simply certainly cut down, because forestry is the action of foresting lumber. If we called it simply the ministry of forests we would begin develop an understanding of how we have to treat our forests in a sustainable manner.
One of the things that awed me as I flew over various parts of British Columbia and had a chance to visit the Kutzamateen and to go to the Carmanah Valley was the sheer beauty, splendour and the age of some of our own forests. We have heard a lot of talk about the Amazonian rain forests and how Canadian and worldwide efforts are being made to save the Amazonian rain forests, but in

Government Orders
our own country there seems to be a lack of understanding of our own capacity to preserve old growth forests.
Let us examine this particular initiative of the government in establishing and putting some emphasis on our forests not only as a unique tool of economic opportunity but also as a unique reflection of our heritage and, I think, a symbol of what our country has been and could be in the future.
If we step back for a moment and begin to re-examine the basic premise of a ministry of forestry and start to integrate some of the findings and understandings that we drew from the United Nations Report on Our Common Future chaired by Madam Brundtland, one of the points made in that particular report and which was certainly re-emphasized in the Liberal Task Force Report on Forests released in March, 1989, is that if we do not properly husband our resources and if we do not properly manage our forests in a way that is sustainable for future generations, while we may be embroiled in short term arguments about the disposition of certain kinds of lumber, we will not have a sustainable resource for future generations.
I was very concerned when I read the bill to discover that there is no specific reference to sustainable development. There is no specific federal mandate on how we can maintain our forests and what percentage of our forests can be reasonably harvested in the short term to guarantee the economic prosperity that we care about, while at the same time making sure that we have a resource for future generations.
I do not see, for example, any discussion about the whole question of the shipping of raw logs. If I look at the report written by, among others, the Member for Kenora-Rainy River, one of our jobs as legislators is obviously to ensure the economic viability of our own communities which is very much dependent on the harvesting of our forests. At the same time we should ensure that our forests are harvested in a manner that is value added. That means jobs for Canadians.
I pointed out an example in my question to an hon. member from British Columbia of one way that is not happening. I sat in the office of the Haida people in the Queen Charlottes and watched two barges go by in the short space of about three or four hours. According to

Those opportunities, bringing departments together, bringing different levels of government together, is where the creativity and the imagination of all of us can come together to develop this industry to secure its past and our future.

Mr. Speaker, I thank the gentleman for his comments with regard to my comments on the forestry department. All of the things that this government is doing are certainly commendable, but surely he is kidding when he cannot recognize the fact that there are millions of dollars cut in the budget in the forestry division, that staffing has been cut back. Where is the dedication? Where is the commitment to this industry when there is a budget cut-back and a person-years cut-back? It is there in the figures. It is in the Minister of Finance's budget.
The member talks about agreements with the provinces. How many of those agreements are not signed? Quite a few. I believe six out of ten are still not signed. We have heard from my colleague from Thunder Bay who talked about the softwood lumber industry and the damage that is being done to the lumber industry in northern Ontario by the 15 per cent surcharge that has been added on. How can he ignore that? How can he say that his government is committed to this industry when he failed to do the things that I have mentioned here?
I would like this gentleman and this government to be serious about this industry. This, I believe, is our No. 2 industry in Canada. It has been our No. 1 industry from the early days of settlers in this country. We cannot ignore it. We cannot ignore the warming effect, the greenhouse effect, on our planet.

Mr. Speaker, in addressing Bill C-29, an act to establish
Government Orders
the department of forestry, to amend the Forestry Development and Research Act and to make related amendments to other acts, I would like to begin by congratulating the minister as another old sawmiller like myself with some 20 years in the industry. I understand also the minister's own commitment and experience in that industry as an owner-operator in his case. I know the two of us share the feeling that comes with the sweet smell of fresh cut wood, especially if it is mixed with salt air.
The minister's own experience in that industry stretches back over many years in the Peace River section of British Columbia. While I never dealt with him directly there, I know that his own experience and feeling both for the industry and the forests that sustain are strong. I know it is of some pleasure and relief to him that he has finally been able to give birth to the measure that is before us today, the establishment of a department of forestry.
In referring to the rather long gestation period, I would point out that in 1984 the Conservative Party and the present minister had some role to play in the forestry policy of that party. They said that we would have a forestry department immediately. It has been five years in coming. By any standard of measurement, that is a rather long gestation period. As one who has been involved in wood products labour for very many years, I always knew that forestry was hard labour, but five years' gestation is kind of ridiculous.
Be that as it may, I know there were many serious debates taking place between parties, between individual members within parties and between many others across the country during that period and the years preceding it over whether the correct and best route to go for the protection and enhancement of the forest industry was to have a separate department, or whether it would be more appropriate to have a ministry with an enhanced associate deputy minister and a strong team within a major government department.
It was also a matter of great concern to a number of others as to what type of department was appropriate if we were to promote and defend properly the interests of the industry and the resource. Should it be a production oriented department or is it more proper to put it in with the Department of the Environment? There were good arguments on all sides, and I think all of us in every party finally came to the conclusion that the best route to go was to have a separate ministry and a separate department.

September 29, 1989
Government Orders
It is regrettable, however, that in establishing this department and for something that has taken so long we find it lacks one of the major instruments that surely any department has as its main purpose-the enhancement and protection of the forestry resource in Canada. The administration of and responsibility for forestry renewal does not rest within the mandate of that department, particularly in the negotiation of and the funding for the joint agreements which have done much during the last four to five years to finally give an appropriate measure of attention to the forest industry and to the forest resource.
In The Vancouver Sun on June 28, 1989, it was reported that officials from the Western Economic Diversification Office told MPs the day before that only $242 million in new money has been made available over the next five years for federal deals with the four western provinces. That much money is to be spread over four western provinces with 11 federal-provincial economic regional agreements. When you consider that during this past five years under FRDA in the province of British Columbia alone, there has been $150 million federal and $150 million provincial, that $242 million is obviously totally inadequate.
If we look at the estimates for the Western Economic Diversification Office, we find that the amount available to that office for its mandate has fallen by $40 million over the period 1988-89 to the 1989-90. Again, this is something that does not bode well. Many spokespersons within the industry and around the industry have suggested that it is entirely inappropriate for an agency such as the western diversification agency to have that kind of responsibility and power over what is in Canada the major contributor to our balance of trade surplus-if it is still a surplus-an industry which has such an impact on so many communities right across Canada, some 300 communities which are either solely or largely dependent upon the forest industry for their existence and welfare.
It is some time now since the first Canadian Forest Congress was held in the city of Toronto in 1978. I was there. It was just shortly after I was appointed as a regional representative for the International Woodworkers of America, not dealing with forestry policy as such,
but with the issue of with race relations within the forest industry.
I remember at that congress in 1978 it was still our concern that there was hardly any awareness among the public of Canada about the importance of this industry and the needs that the forest resource had. A phrase used was that the public could not see the lack of forest for the trees.
We have come a long way since then and there is a great deal of awareness among the public and among the people who work in and around the industry. Over the years that has created an ever-increasing sense of urgency in the political area as well.
While the creation of this department is obviously one sign of that increasing awareness among politicians as with the public, it is likely to be a long time before we can again focus public attention on another major step ahead in terms of the renewal of the forest resource in Canada. That is why it grieves me so much to see the lack of a strong mandate written into the legislation before us. It is a pity because it may be a long way away again. It has taken five years to get us this far from the time of the announcement that it was going to be done immediately. If we do not do it right now it may be a long, long time before we get a chance again.
As I said, Mr. Speaker, there are some 300 communities across Canada dependent upon the forest industry and many of them are within my own constituency of Kootenay West-Revelstoke. I know the figure 300 was used in a broad sense some four or five years ago, at the time that I was the member for Kootenay West, and since then we have at least one less community in my own area that is primarily dependent upon that industry. The mill where I reported to go back to work, some two weeks after the 1984 election, closed down permanently within days of my application to return to work. I was one of those who thought he had job security when I left this place in 1984, but I should have known better because I had realized for years and years that unless all people have job security no one has it. But I was rather forcibly reminded of that in the weeks following the election of 1984, and it had nothing to do with losing the election.

Now the employment within my own constituency within the forest industry is not much different than it was then. But what has happened there, as has happened in many other communities, is that many large, integrated operations have closed down. We have gone back to the days of a number of small operations which have much more hazardous working conditions. In many cases they conduct their logging operations in ways which are much less sensitive to the needs of the area. They pay their employees and thus pay their communities less for the resources that they utilize. They now have people working with them who are working for one-half or two-thirds of the wages that they used to earn. They have no benefits, except for those few required by law, and have no pensions. We have gone backwards in terms of what our people and our communities receive from that industry in many, many areas of Canada. And that in part is because of the small "c" conservative political agenda which has dominated much of North America over that period.
We hear a lot of concern about the environment. That is right and proper and it is long overdue. But I have always been one who believed that the environment had to do with more than just trees, minerals, air and water. People are part of the environment too; people tomorrow and people today. The job of any responsible politician and any responsible government is to accommodate and negotiate between those needs of people today and people tomorrow, recognizing that they are part of what we call the environment and ensuring that one is not sacrificed in too large a measure for the benefit of another.
In addressing part of the needs of the people, and there are hundreds and thousands of them across this country who have derived their livelihood from the harvesting of our forests, if we want to enlist them as allies which we must in preserving forests and in preserving the environment we must assure and guarantee to them some fair measure of equity. We cannot ask them simply to sacrifice themselves, their families and their communities for the future.
It is important that sacrifices be made but they must be shared. We must apportion to them in our reforestation and silvicultural programs an appropriate number of the
Government Orders
jobs at reasonable rates of pay with appropriate compensation. benefits and pensions for the future of themselves and their families working in those important areas of silviculture and forestry regeneration.
If we do not make those assurances, they will automatically dig in their heels and we will force the kinds of social conflicts that we have seen in the headlines over and over and over again. Our society cannot afford those conflicts on an ever-increasing basis. Our environment cannot sustain those conflicts on an ever-increasing basis and it is within our ability, as a community provincially, nationally and locally, to take such measures to ensure that any sacrifices to be made will be shared equitably across the board and that we will give as much respect and accord to those who are living and working in the present as to the future.
I have always been suspicious, whether it has been with other Socialists, Conservatives or Liberals, of any politician who says that we always have to do things for tomorrow at the expense of those today. We are equally as important. Besides, if we do not take both groups equally into account we will not take the kinds of measures that are necessary to preserve a future existence.
I know that a lot has been said about the FRDA agreement over the last five years and it has been an excellent agreement. I have had the opportunity, both formerly as a member of Parliament and during my four years in the wilderness, as it were, to visit a number of operations that were financed both by FRDA and by the agreements that were conducted prior to the existence of the Forest Renewal Development Agreements.
I can testify to the value of the work being done with minimal amounts of labour and, considering the importance of this industry and this resource, our forests, with the minimal amount of money spent we got tremendous value in terms of enhancement of the resource.
There was something that went on prior to the last five-year FRDA agreement in British Columbia. The B.C.-Canada FRDA agreement had $150 million federal and $150 million provincial, a total of $300 million over five years. That is some $30 million a year for each level of government.

September 29, 1989
Government Orders
I would remind the members opposite that in the year prior to FRDA there was an agreement for which we had to fight for years to get. It was a one year agreement. There is a problem with short-term agreements. The five-year one was certainly welcome in that respect. It takes a lot of planning and co-ordination. There was a one-year agreement that saw $55 million dollars come from the federal government and $55 million from the province.
So in fact, if you measure it on that year-by-year basis, when this government was elected in 1984, its commitment fell from $55 million a year to $30 million a year. But the government probably got just as good a value because it was at least planned over a five-year period. That allowed the provincial authorities who have the prime jurisdiction, as they should, over forest management and forest renewal to plan in advance to attempt to get the appropriate number of seedlings in place, to do the necessary preparatory work and to have the necessary skilled labour in place, because we had not done an adequate job of reforestation prior to that time and we needed to train forestry technicians and silviculturalists. It allowed that to happen. But because of the foot dragging in this last year we have thrown away the benefits of that kind of advance planning.
Even if the federal government were now to agree to spend more than it had over the past five years, when all the evidence shows it is going to spend less, it would get fewer results and do great damage to our resource simply because of the lack of lead time. Seedlings have not been produced, not adequate ones for the right places. Because of the privatization program that has taken place in the province of British Columbia where many of the seedlings are produced by independent contractors, largely made up of former employees of that province, they are left holding the bag, otherwise the taxpayers would have ended up holding the bag. It would have been unfair to the taxpayers and it is now unfair to those contractors, because these seedlings will probably not be used.
That shows the waste. You would think that a government that had shown enough sense to do things over a five-year period where the appropriate amount of planning could take place would realize how important it is
for that kind of planning on a long sustained basis to continue, but apparently it has not.
Now we are seeing jurisdiction not placed within the new ministry of forests but placed in another agency which may be very valuable, the Western Diversification Fund. But it has different priorities. It does not have the understanding of the particular problems of that industry, so we can expect to see even more of that helter-skelter unplanned approach because these people simply will not understand the industry. You do not plan to regenerate a forest in one year or one month. You have to do it over the long haul. I am sure the minister understands that. If he does, why does he not get it through the thick skulls of his colleagues? He knows what the necessities are and knows the urgency. I only wish his other colleagues would come to appreciate the particular needs of that industry.
Another disturbing trend has been in what we are now starting to see as some hints of Conservative plans to deal with forestry and some of the broad environmental concerns. The Conservatives and Liberals have been urging so-called market-driven solutions to our environment. But it is market mechanisms that have got us in the situation we are in now. As an example, according to the September 23 issue of The Financial Post, Environment Probe in Toronto is calling for the privatization of our-

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext:
Order, please. The Chair regrets to interrupt the member but the member's time has expired.
On debate, the Hon. Member for Winnipeg South Centre.

Mr. Speaker, I want to make the time available to me this afternoon to pose some questions to the House and in particular the proposed minister of forestry.
What Canadians want to know before this bill is passed is whether this is another mechanism to get the minister a bigger car, a better seat at the cabinet table, a larger expense account and a little more status among his colleagues or whether the forestry department is now going to do something. They want to know whether, in fact, it is going to be a real, substantial contribution to the making of proper policy in this country dealing with forests which is, after all, our largest employer and our most successful export market in many areas.

The forest industry is in deep trouble as a direct consequence of actions by this government. The real question is whether this new ministry of forestry and the new minister is going to be prepared to stand up finally with some courage and integrity and defend the forestry industry of Canada.
I hear comments from the gentleman who represents that large forestry area in Mississauga or Scarborough, wherever it is.
The fact of the matter is I have here a study done by Price Waterhouse for the forest industry in British Columbia. This is an objective, honest and clear account of just what disastrous effects the decisions by this government have had upon the forestry industry in British Columbia. Let me read you one quite startling fact: "In 1988 the net earnings of the industry in the lumber field alone plummeted from $352 million to $6 million."
The direct consequence of the softwood lumber agreement, the export tax, the stumpage fees, has been the cause of that decline. The lumber industry is losing markets and has increased costs and, as a result, it is losing money. When it loses money the industry loses the capital to reinvest in modernization. It loses the ability to provide for better technology, higher productivity and, therefore, loses what has been for the British Columbia forest industry perhaps its most important advantage, namely, its superior ability to produce logs at lower cost, at higher productivity and with better technology. Once it starts losing money of this scope and magnitude it loses its cutting edge, if you don't mind a somewhat bad pun.
That is not a matter of nature, it is not God's will, it is a direct decision by this government. One of the stupidest, most futile and dishonest decisions in the history of trade in this country is now coming home to roost and we are seeing the impact directly in British Columbia, northern Ontario and right across this country. What was a thriving, bountiful industry is now being put into real dilemma as to its future and as to whether it can continue to provide for an active export market.
There is a responsibility by the minister of forestry because his colleagues have failed. The Minister for International Trade, who somehow has believed that his primary occupation these days is to provide for the destruction of the fish industry off the east coast, has failed miserably in his primary responsibility, which is to do something about the trade area.
Government Orders
I want to quote from the Minister for International Trade on April 7, 1989, just a few short months ago. He said: "The economic circumstances (for the forest industry) have changed-Therefore we think it would be reasonable for changes to be made-Whether the United States will agree is another question. We have pointed out these facts..(but) there have been no formal negotiations-".
I checked a few days ago and there are still no negotiations. There is still no initiative by the minister for trade. There is still no honest effort to try to come to grips with the fact that the Canadian forest industry faces the drastic impact of new stumpage fees in British Columbia and the export tax in the other provinces, to say nothing of the major increase in the Canadian dollar.
I have a very simple question for the minister of forestry. Once his department is there, once he gets in the harness, once he gets that bigger car and that new staff and all the trappings, is he going to start renegotiating this agreement? Is he going to tackle the fundamental flaw that faces the Canadian forestry industry? Rather than going out and making great speeches about the green ghetto and all the nice pieces of nostalgia he liked to refer to in his opening speeches, is he going to do something serious? Is he really going to tackle the problem that faces the industry which he knows well? I was within three feet of his office only a few days ago, and there they were busy, the computers were whirring, and the typewriters were going. But I have not seen the minister whirring and going. I want to know if we are going to get some action once this department is passed and if, for a change, we are going to have a minister in this government to stand up to the Americans, someone who is going to stand up for Canadian industry and say let us start doing some serious negotiation.
It is not a matter of changing policy. Even his colleague, the minister of trade, when we can find him, is prepared to admit that there is a serious problem. He knows that negotiations have to take place, he knows that something has to happen, but he is incapable of doing it. I know that the Minister of Forestry with his new department deeply cares about his region-he had better or he will not get elected next time-but aside from that, his own sense of humanity and well-being would require him to do something. Is he going to do it, or is he going to find himself, once again, captive to that peculiar paranoia that is so omnipresent, so totally in existence on the other side that people are fearful of

Government Orders
standing up on behalf of this country and its major industry?
If they do not, Mr. Speaker, this industry is going to be facing increasingly tougher times. As international competition gets tougher and tougher the industry will find itself without the capital. There is a capital grab by the province of British Columbia. There is an export tax which steals it from the saw mills in northern Ontario and prairie regions of Canada.
That is the primary task. I am more than happy to relinquish my remaining few minutes to the Minister of Forestry if he is prepared to say here and now publicly that that will be his first priority, that the minute he is given the new baton of office and the door is open, he is going to buy himself an air ticket to Washington and start saying to the Americans: "The game is over. We have had enough fun and games with this particular little jaunt. You have now been able to exploit us for three years. Is it not time we got down and did something honest and even?". Is the Minister of Forestry now prepared to say that he will undertake that kind of initiative?
I would even recommend, as a member of the opposition, that when the minister leaves Washington, he buys a ticket to Tokyo and starts renegotiating the decision dealing with the Japanese tariffs on lumber. Perhaps he would do the full world-wide tour and hit Geneva where he will make an appeal against that decision, so we can again open up the Japanese market and not lose it on a technicality. I will not blame the government for making the odd technical mistake. However, the government makes more than the odd mistake. It makes them about 100 times a day.
We lost that case with Japan on a technical argument. It is going to take some initiative, motivation, and some minister with will, purpose, energy, thought and creativity, to start representing this area rather than just occupying a warm seat around the cabinet table.
This is not based upon what might have been. This is based upon hard fact. I recall very well one of the minister's predecessors, the since retired Minister for International Trade, who negotiated that softwood lumber agreement in tough battles on the beaches of Hawaii, fighting for Canadians every moment as she dashed
herself with suntan lotion. She said this would be the greatest thing that ever happened to the lumber industry. This would solve our problems. Do you recall what she said, Mr. Speaker? You were in the house. She said: "This is a great victory for Canada". Well, Mr. Speaker, you convince the lumber industry that has just lost $352 million last year in net earnings that this is a great victory for Canada.
I simply say to the minister, who I am pleased to see is in the house, that he knows what his job is. I do not say that it is an easy task. I am here simply to urge him and to pray with him that he will take it on. Unless there is a change made, unless we can get a renegotiation of that agreement, unless we can end that agreement, then the future of the forest industry is dim indeed.
For all the other rhetoric that he may provide, and for all the other speeches and policy papers that he may want to introduce, until he addresses himself and his government to the single most serious problem facing the forest industry, he will not have done his job.
Therefore, Mr. Speaker, we in the opposition will wait with interest to see if this new ministry of forestry is simply a hollow shell providing more creature comforts for the minister of forestry or whether in fact it will do something serious about tackling a problem facing one of the most important industries in Canada.

Mr. Speaker, I am honoured to have an opportunity to participate in today's debate on this most important legislation. We see before us Bill C-29, an act to establish the department of forestry. I say thank you to the minister. We have waited years and years and years for this. Finally, the government was embarrassed enough to have to do something. I want to say to the Minister of Forestry who is here with us that I remember vividly as a matter of fact way back in March, 1984, when our Prime Minister stated the following: "As a government we would create a department of forestry in order to ensure that the problems now facing this industry are dealt with before it is too late." That was in 1984. We waited all of 1984, all of 1985, all of 1986, all of 1987, and here we are, Mr. Speaker, and finally the government is now going to introduce legislation. Well, I tell you, Mr. Speaker, and my hon. friend from Winnipeg who just spoke on behalf of the Liberal Party, we waited decades, of course, and never had anything at all from

the Liberals on this initiative. So I think that their criticisms are somewhat hollow.
As a matter of fact, if my memory serves me, and I believe that it does accurately, when the Leader of the Official Opposition was visiting Prince George, British Columbia, he indicated that it was Liberal policy not to establish a department of forests, that it ought to be within a larger umbrella of industrial development. I simply point that out to my hon. friend from Winnipeg in case that slipped his mind.
Obviously what we are seeing here is an issue that is not a high priority. If it is a high priority, the government would have moved back in 1984, 1985,1986,1987 or 1988. It is not a high priority. So let us hope that once we get this legislation in place the Minister of Forests will actually start treating the forest industry as he ought.
When you consider the number of people who are directly and indirectly employed in this industry, which is in excess of 800,000, when you recognize that more than 300 communities in this country depend exclusively on the forest industry for their economic base, and when you recognize that in terms of Canada's trade it is forestry and forest products that are at the top of the list and so critical in terms of our foreign trade, we have to hope now that it becomes somewhat of a priority because it certainly has not been one up until this point.
I must say that the creation of a forestry department is welcome news. Obviously, when one looks carefully through Bill C-29 we find that it is woefully inadequate. We see that it is certainly an opening now. It provides us as parliamentarians with a window of opportunity to not simply accept this bill, which is inadequate in so many ways, but to enhance it now through an appropriate set of amendments. Our forestry spokesman, the hon. member from Prince George-Bulkley Valley, has already outlined carefully what we would like to see as ways and means of enhancing this legislation.
I simply want to refer to them because I think it is critical that the Minister of Forests know right at this point, at least some of the major initiatives that we are going to propose. One, of course, is adding to the annual report provisions. When you see in the legislation that there will be an annual report, unfortunately, it will be
Government Orders
like most annual reports of most departments, a glowing comment about the wonderful minister and the wonderful people involved-utter and total propaganda nonsense by and large. This is too serious to play politics with, as we have seen played too often in these annual reports.
Therefore, we are going to include some amendments to the legislation to ensure that the annual report reflect and give us an update on the forest inventory across the country, the employment statistics, the number of jobs created and developed in the various sectors, the most recent trade figures, as well as outlining and suggesting a number of new initiatives and proposals for the forthcoming year. These are simply a number of things we would like to see in the annual report. We want to see this legislation to ensure that we do not get just some namby-pamby propaganda.
Second, we feel that it is appropriate that in the legislation itself there be a call for a First Ministers' Conference on the forest industry each year. Let us face it. There is no more important sector when you consider that people in every single province and in every single territory are involved in this industry. There are hundreds of thousands of people directly involved in this industry. Is it too much to ask that our Prime Minister and the first ministers of each province and territory get together and discuss the challenges facing this critical sector on a five-year basis? We figure that is important.
Then, of course, the ministers of forestry ought to get together every year to discuss the challenges facing the industry and to identify solutions to those challenges.
Also, we want to propose the establishment of a forest trade commissioner. After all, I think we all recognize that now in our shakes and shingles industry 90 per cent of it goes into foreign markets. A good portion of our pulp and paper, lumber and plywood is taking advantage of newly developing foreign markets, but there is much that can be done. There are many more initiatives that we ought to be taking in terms of selling our products which are top rate, top of the line, first rate overseas. We would like to suggest that a forest trade commissioner would be a step in advancing that type of initiative.

September 29, 1989
Government Orders
I think also that we need in this legislation provisions that will ensure new jobs are created in this industry. We often look about the country and ask ourselves how could we put more Canadians to work meaningfully. I do not mean snap your finger and create a job schemes that are good for maybe three or four months or whatever. We have seen those in the past. That is not the solution in terms of full-time employment opportunities.
It is interesting that in the central interior of British Columbia, and the Minister would certainly be aware of this, a number of municipalities have commissioned studies to look to see what needs to be done in terms of enhancing that forest resource and how many jobs would be created as a result. The figures are absolutely astounding. If we were doing in our country what we should be doing, that is, enhancing, developing and nurturing our forest resource which means thinning, spacing and fertilizing and impending programs for disease, fire and pest control, road building, research and development, and so on, there are tens of thousands of jobs that could be developed, if we are serious about sustaining that forest resource.
These are long-term jobs. If you take the central part of British Columbia alone, there are literally thousands of jobs that could be developed to enhance that forest resource. I cannot think of a better investment. Rather than provide money for various income support programs, whether it is welfare on one hand or unemployment insurance on the other, if we could take that same initiative and develop hundreds and thousands of jobs that must be developed. This is not something that could be or should be. It must be. We have no alternative.
We say this is what should be done in this legislation to implement programs in terms of proper tree planting. We cannot do it overnight. We recognize that. We certainly ought to have a crash program put into place because there are many people who understand the wood industry. They have lost their jobs over the years and could very quickly put that expertise and experience to work, to say nothing of the thousands of experienced tree planters who would enjoy working full time in
developing the forest resources of the country. We put that as a very high priority in terms of amendments that my hon. friend from Prince George-Bulkley Valley will be providing once we get into the committee stage.
I also want to refer to the FRDAs. I have here the Forest Resource Development Agreement between Canada and British Columbia. I notice that it expires in March 1990. Just a few months from now it will expire.
Many of us from British Columbia are becoming quite concerned with this expiry date approaching because we have noticed that when these agreements expired in Alberta, Saskatchewan and Manitoba the government did not renew them. They just said: "That's it, we are going to abandon the forest industry. We are going to abandon working with the provinces to enhance the forest resource in Alberta, Saskatchewan and Manitoba". Here is British Columbia coming up next.
What this means-the writing is clearly on the wall-is that this government has no plans to sign a new agreement between British Columbia and the federal government to enhance and support the forest industry. This is critical, of course, in a province where the forest industry is the number one economic sector.
We would suggest that the government show that this matter of the forest industry is a priority. It should commit immediately to signing a new agreement with the provinces by which the federal government and the provincial governments can develop a long-term forestry strategy to ensure that the forest industry not only is maintained in a healthy condition but is going to be there for future generations. This of course means that we have to spend some time developing those lands that have not be sufficiently planted. We have got thousands and tens of thousands of hectares of forest land that we refer to as NSR, non-satisfactory restocked lands. These are forest lands where companies have gone in, usually clear cut, logged off all the trees and just left. If that is not insanity, I do not know what is. Other forest producing nations look at us, scratch their heads and think we must be crazy to cut down tress and not restock the land. That is exactly what has been done.
September 29, 1989

British Columbia, of course, had the very unfortunate experience to say to the forest industry: "We want you to monitor what you are doing. We want you to be seif-policing. We want you to be self-managing". They tried that for a year. The results were so dramatically negative that they have had to renege on that. This makes the case that legislation at the provincial and federal level is critical if we are going to maintain that forest resource.
Up until now the province of British Columbia and Canada had an agreement which involved $300 million over five years for reforestation and silviculture. That is $30 million a year, which I think is a pittance. I think if we are serious we have got to increase this, say, to a $1 billion over the next five to ten years.
Why not?

The minister says: "Why not?" I applaud him for that comment. Why not spend that kind of money and put a few tens of thousands of Canadians to work meaningfully? You might ask where are we going to get $1 billion. May I suggest where? By implementing a minimum corporate tax like they have done in the United States. It would generate a few billion dollars each year by doing what President Reagan did in 1986. He introduced a minimum corporate tax because he felt that if you have as we have in Canada tens of thousands of corporations that do not pay any income tax at all they should pay their fair share. They should not pay too much or excessively; they should pay something. It is unfair when the welding shop down at the comer of the street is paying tax but the Royal Bank of Canada or General Motors pays no tax. We in the New Democratic Party say that is unfair.
If the Minister is looking for a source of revenue so that in fact he could put $1 billion into the agreements between Canada and the province of British Columbia over a five to ten year period, may I suggest that that is one place where he can start to look.
I also want to make a point, and I say this as an honorary member of IWA Canada Local 1-417, that it is time that we stopped expecting those people involved in the forest industry to pay for our parks, to pay for our wilderness areas and our recreational lands. If we as a country want, and we should want, wilderness areas set aside, parks set aside, conservation areas set aside, which are laudable and necessary goals for our country-we have even set 12 per cent as a guideline in terms of lands that should be set aside for these uses-then it should
not be those people employed in the woods industry that should pay for this. It should be society that pays for this.
We need to find some mechanism to put in place so that it is not pitting those companies and workers in the forest industry against those people who want to set aside these lands for uses other than forestry. We need, if I can use the parlance of the free trade deal, a dispute settlement mechanism whereby we can have a process, if there is a dispute over the future of certain lands that could be harvested for forest industry reasons, to get away from emotionalism and have reasonable decision making brought forward. Then we can have, if you like, lands that will be harvested in terms of the forest industry and other lands that will be set aside for wilderness conservation and park zones.
I think this is becoming paramount. This emotional crisis that we have to deal with on a valley to valley basis must stop in this country. I would like to see the minister of forests, as a result of the development of this new ministry, playing a leadership role. If he could do that in the next three years he would be making quite a contribution to this country. I will tell you that my hon. colleague from Prince George-Bulkley Valley will be urging him at every opportunity to do just that.
If this is the kind of leadership that we can expect from the federal government? A lot of people ask: "What is the role of the federal government in terms of the forest industry?" After all, our Constitution gives this area, if you like, to the provinces. It places resource development and so on under provincial jurisdiction.
There are all kinds of initiatives that can be taken. I have identified research and development. I have identified the whole matter of leadership and partnership in reforestation and silviculture. If we had in our country a long-term agreed upon forest strategy involving those people employed in the industry, the investors, the regional governments, local governments, provincial governments and federal governments, can you imagine what kind of a dynamic forest industry we could have in this country? But that requires leadership.
I am pleased to say that Bill C-29, an act to establish the department of forestry, is a step toward establishing and accepting that leadership role. I encourage all of us to do whatever we can as we develop this legislation in the next number of weeks to rally around, to not only introduce this legislation which is pretty weak, inadequate and lacking but to develop a bill and to develop the resulting department of forestry that actually will accomplish what every single thoughtful parliamentarian
